nodes.name: Willmore surface / Willmore functional
nodes.statement: A Willmore surface is, by definition, a critical point of the Willmore functional $$ \mathcal{W}(\Sigma) = \int_\Sigma H^2 \,d\mu $$ where $H=\frac{1}{2}(k_1+k_2)$ is the mean curvature, $k_1,k_2$ are the principal curvatures and where $d\mu$ denotes the associated volume form of the surface.
nodes.statement_short: A Willmore surface is a critical point of the total squared mean curvature $\mathcal{W}(\Sigma)=\int_\Sigma H^2\,d\mu$.
nodes.genus: critical point of the Willmore functional

nodes.name: elastic curve (elastica) in the hyperbolic plane
nodes.statement: It it known \cite{LanSing_Curves_in_the} that Willmore surfaces of revolution are generated by elastic curves in the hyperbolic plane $\Hh$ (called elasticae), which, by definition, are critical for the total squared curvature functional.
nodes.statement_short: Elasticae are curves in $\Hh$ that are critical for the total squared curvature functional; they generate Willmore surfaces of revolution.
nodes.origin_citation: Langer & Singer, Curves in the hyperbolic plane
nodes.genus: elastic curves in the hyperbolic plane $\Hh$
differentia: critical for the total squared curvature functional

nodes.name: surface of revolution $\Sigma_\gamma$ generated by an elastica
nodes.statement: The surface then takes the form \begin{equation} \Sigma_\gamma = \Big\{ (\gamma_1(s),\gamma_2(s)\cos(t),\gamma_2(s)\sin(t)) : s\in I, t\in [0,2\pi) \Big\} \end{equation} where $I\subset\R$ is some interval und $\gamma$ is an elastic curve in the hyperbolic plane.
nodes.statement_short: $\Sigma_\gamma$ is the surface obtained by revolving the planar curve $\gamma$ about the $x_1$-axis.

nodes.name: symmetric / nonsymmetric solution of the Dirichlet problem
nodes.statement: Here, a solution of \eqref{eq:DirichletBVP} is called symmetric if we have $$ \gamma_1(L/2+s)=-\gamma_1(L/2-s),\quad \gamma_2(L/2+s)=\gamma_1(L/2-s) \qquad\text{for all }s\in [0,L/2] $$ and it is called nonsymmetric otherwise.
nodes.statement_short: A solution is symmetric when $\gamma$ is odd/even about the midpoint $s=L/2$ of its length.

nodes.name: positive / negative orientation of an elastica
nodes.statement: Positive / negative orientation means that the hyperbolic curvature of the elastica is assumed to be positive / negative at some point (and hence everywhere since the $\dn$-function is zero-free).
differentia: the hyperbolic curvature of the elastica is assumed to be positive / negative at some point

nodes.name: the hyperbolic plane $\Hh$, its metric and its distance function
nodes.statement: Willmore surfaces of revolution are known to be generated by elastic curves in the hyperbolic plane $\mathbb{H}=\{(x_1,x_2)\in\R^2: x_2>0\}$, see for instance p.532 in \cite{LanSing_Curves_in_the}. The metric is given by $\frac{dx_1^2+dx_2^2}{x_2^2}$ and the distance between two points $(x_1,x_2),(y_1,y_2)\in \Hh$ is \begin{equation} d_{\Hh}((x_1,x_2),(y_1,y_2)) = \Arcosh\Big(1+\frac{(x_1-y_1)^2+(x_2-y_2)^2}{2x_2y_2}\Big). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: The upper half plane $\Hh=\{x_2>0\}$ with metric $(dx_1^2+dx_2^2)/x_2^2$ and the associated $\Arcosh$ distance formula.
nodes.origin_citation: Langer & Singer, Curves in the hyperbolic plane, p.532

nodes.name: parametrization by hyperbolic arclength
nodes.statement: Regular curves $\gamma$ in $\Hh$ are therefore parametrized by hyperbolic arclength if $(\gamma_1')^2+(\gamma_2')^2\equiv \gamma_2^2$ and in fact all curves studied in this paper will be written down in this parametrization.

nodes.name: angle function $\phi$ and hyperbolic (geodesic) curvature $\kappa$
nodes.statement: Introducing the angle function $\phi$ via $\gamma_1' = \gamma_2 \cos(\phi),\gamma_2' = \gamma_2 \sin(\phi)$ (such that $\gamma'=|\gamma'|e^{i\phi}$) one finds that the hyperbolic (or geodesic) curvature function is given by \begin{equation} \kappa := - \frac{\gamma_2^2}{\gamma_2'} \Big(\frac{\gamma_1'}{\gamma_2^2}\Big)' = \phi'+\cos(\phi). \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: $\phi$ is defined by $\gamma'=|\gamma'|e^{i\phi}$ and the hyperbolic curvature is $\kappa=\phi'+\cos(\phi)$.

nodes.name: orbitlike elastica
nodes.statement: Following \cite{LanSing_Curves_in_the} (not necessarily closed) elastic curves generated by such curvature functions will be called orbitlike.
nodes.origin_citation: Langer & Singer, Curves in the hyperbolic plane

nodes.name: the conformal invariant $Z(s;P)$
nodes.statement: The key to achieve this goal is a thorough discussion of the function \begin{equation} Z(s;P) = \frac{(\gamma_1(s)-P_1)^2+(\gamma_2(s)-P_2)^2}{2P_2\gamma_2(s)} \qquad\text{for all } P=(P_1,P_2)\in \C \text{ with }P_2\neq 0, \end{equation} which for $P\in\Hh$ is a conformal invariant due to $d_{\Hh}(\gamma(s),P) = \Arcosh(1+Z(s;P))$, see~\eqref{eq:metric}.
nodes.statement_short: $Z(\cdot;P)$ encodes the hyperbolic distance to $P$ via $d_{\Hh}(\gamma(s),P)=\Arcosh(1+Z(s;P))$.
nodes.section: 3 Classification of elasticae in the hyperbolic plane

nodes.name: the names circular, orbitlike, geodesic and wavelike elasticae
nodes.statement: These figures motivate the names (i) circular, (ii) orbitlike, (iii) geodesic / asymptotically geodesic or (iv) wavelike, respectively.
nodes.section: 3 Classification of elasticae in the hyperbolic plane
nodes.definiendum: circular, orbitlike, geodesic / asymptotically geodesic, wavelike

nodes.name: elliptic integrals of the first and second kind $F,E$ and the complete elliptic integrals $K,E$
nodes.statement: The elliptic integrals of the first and second kind are defined by $$ F(l,k) := \int_0^l \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-t^2}\sqrt{1-k^2t^2}}\,dt, \qquad E(l,k) := \int_0^l \frac{\sqrt{1-k^2t^2}}{\sqrt{1-t^2}}\,dt $$ and in the special case $l=1$ we obtain the so-called complete elliptic integrals $K(k) := F(1,k)$, $E(k) := E(1,k)$.
nodes.definiendum: elliptic integrals of the first and second kind

nodes.name: Jacobi's elliptic functions $\sn,\cn,\dn$
nodes.statement: As we will see in \eqref{eq:Jac_Inverse} these functions relate to Jacobi's elliptic functions $\sn(\cdot,k),\cn(\cdot,k),\dn(\cdot,k)$ (we omit the arguments for convenience) that can be defined as the unique solution of the initial value problem \begin{align} \sn' = \cn\dn, \quad \cn'=-\sn\dn,\quad \dn' = -k^2\sn\cn,\quad \sn(0)=0,\;\cn(0)=\dn(0)=1. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: $\sn,\cn,\dn$ are defined as the unique solution of a first-order ODE system with $\sn(0)=0,\cn(0)=\dn(0)=1$.
nodes.genus: the unique solution of the initial value problem

nodes.name: Heuman's Lambda function $\Lambda_0$
nodes.statement: Next we define Heuman's Lambda function $\Lambda_0$ via $$ \Lambda_0(\arcsin(l),k):=\frac{2}{\pi} (E(k)F(l,k')+K(k)E(l,k')-K(k)F(l,k')), $$ see 150.03 in \cite{ByrFri_handbook}. Here and in the text we will write $k':=\sqrt{1-k^2}$.

nodes.name: Jacobi's eta, theta and zeta functions $H,\Theta,\Theta_1,\zeta$
nodes.statement: Additionally, we will need Jacobi's eta, theta and zeta functions $H,\Theta,\Theta_1,\zeta:\C\times(0,1)\to\C$ defined through the following formulas (see 144.01 and 1050.01 in \cite{ByrFri_handbook}): \begin{align*} &\Theta(z,k) := \vartheta_0(\frac{\pi z}{2 K(k)},q_k), &&H(z,k) := \vartheta_1(\frac{\pi z}{2 K(k)},q_k), \\ &\Theta_1(z,k) := \vartheta_3(\frac{\pi z}{2 K(k)},q_k), &&\zeta(z,k) := \frac{\Theta_z(z,k)}{\Theta(z,k)}. \end{align*}
nodes.definiendum: Jacobi's eta, theta and zeta functions $H,\Theta,\Theta_1,\zeta:\C\times(0,1)\to\C$

nodes.name: the Jacobian Theta functions $\vartheta_0,\vartheta_1,\vartheta_3$ and the elliptic nome $q_k$
nodes.statement: Here, the Jacobian Theta Functions $\vartheta_0,\vartheta_1$ and the elliptic nome $q_k$ are given by \begin{align} \begin{aligned} \vartheta_0(z,q) &= 1 + 2 \sum_{n=1}^\infty (-1)^n q^{n^2}\cos(2nz), \\ \vartheta_1(z,q) &= 2 \sum_{n=0}^\infty (-1)^n q^{(n+1/2)^2}\sin((2n+1)z), \\ \vartheta_3(z,q) &= 1 + 2\sum_{n=1}^\infty q^{n^2}\cos(2nz), \\ q_k &= \exp(-\pi K(k')/K(k)). \end{aligned} \end{align}
nodes.definiendum: Jacobian Theta Functions $\vartheta_0,\vartheta_1$ and the elliptic nome $q_k$

nodes.name: the rotation $\Delta\theta_k$
nodes.statement: In order to measure the angular progress of an elastica generated by this curvature function via \eqref{eq:ODE_solution} we will need \begin{equation} \Delta\theta_k := \pi- \pi \Lambda_0(\arcsin(k'),k) + 2\sqrt{1-k^2}\sqrt{2-k^2}K(k), \end{equation} a function that has been introduced and analyzed in Proposition 5.3 in~\cite{LanSing_the_total}.
nodes.statement_short: $\Delta\theta_k$ measures the angular progress of an orbitlike elastica over one period of its curvature.
nodes.origin_citation: Langer & Singer, the total squared curvature, Proposition 5.3

nodes.name: the functions $W_1,W_2$ (orbitlike case)
nodes.statement: Now, being given $w_1,w_2$ we define \begin{align} W_j(s) := \frac{1}{\sqrt{2-k^2}} w_j\big(-K(k)+ \frac{s+s_*}{\sqrt{2-k^2}}\big) \qquad (j=1,2). \end{align}

nodes.name: the angle function $\vartheta$ (orbitlike case)
nodes.statement: Next we choose an angle function $\vartheta$ as follows: \begin{align} W_2(s)-iW_1(s) = \frac{ \sqrt{\kappa^2-\mu}}{\kappa} e^{i\vartheta(s)}. \end{align} This definition makes sense due to Proposition~\ref{prop:W1W2_orbitlike}~(i). Notice that \eqref{eq:def_theta} determines $\vartheta$ only up to additive multiples of $2\pi$ so that we require $\vartheta$ to satisfy the inequality $-2\pi<\vartheta(-s_*)\leq 0$.
nodes.statement_short: $\vartheta$ is the argument of $W_2-iW_1$, normalized by $-2\pi<\vartheta(-s_*)\le 0$.

nodes.name: the auxiliary vector fields $\xi^1,\xi^2,\xi^3$
nodes.statement: In order to accurately describe the function $Z$ we will need the following functions: \begin{align} \begin{aligned} \xi^1(s) &:= \matII{ W_1(s)}{W_2(s)}{ W_1'(s)}{ W_2'(s)}^{-1} \vecII{\frac{1}{\kappa(s)}-\frac{\kappa(s)}{\mu}-\frac{\kappa'(s)}{\mu}\sin(\phi(s)) +\frac{\kappa(s)^2}{2\mu}\cos(\phi(s))}{-\frac{1}{\kappa(s)}\sin(\phi(s))-\frac{\kappa'(s)}{\kappa(s)^2}}, \\ \xi^2(s) &:= \matII{ W_1(s)}{ W_2(s)}{ W_1'(s)}{ W_2'(s)}^{-1} \vecII{\frac{1}{\kappa(s)}-\frac{\kappa(s)}{\mu}+\frac{\kappa'(s)}{\mu}\sin(\phi(s)) -\frac{\kappa(s)^2}{2\mu}\cos(\phi(s))}{\frac{1}{\kappa(s)}\sin(\phi(s))-\frac{\kappa'(s)}{\kappa(s)^2}}, \\ \xi^3(s) &:= \matII{ W_1(s)}{ W_2(s)}{ W_1'(s)}{ W_2'(s)}^{-1} \vecII{\frac{\kappa(s)^2}{2\mu}\sin(\phi(s)) +\frac{\kappa'(s)}{\mu}\cos(\phi(s))}{\frac{1}{\kappa(s)}\cos(\phi(s))}. \end{aligned} \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: $\xi^1,\xi^2,\xi^3$ are the $\mathcal{W}^{-1}$-transformed coefficient vectors appearing in the formula for $Z$.

nodes.name: the parameter $k_{m,n}$
nodes.statement: Therefore we define $k_{m,n}\in (0,1)$ to be the unique solution of the equation \begin{equation} \Delta\theta_k = \frac{2\pi m}{n} \end{equation} where $m,n\in\N$ are natural numbers such that $1<\frac{2m}{n}<\sqrt 2$, see Proposition~\ref{prop:rotation}.
nodes.statement_short: $k_{m,n}$ is the unique modulus with $\Delta\theta_k=2\pi m/n$.

nodes.name: the closed elastica $\gamma_{m,n}$
nodes.statement: The associated elastica with initial conditions $\gamma_1(0)=0,\gamma_2(0)=1,\phi(0)=0$ and $s_*=0$, say, will be denoted by $\gamma_{m,n}$. Notice that this choice is somewhat arbitrary since in fact none of the following results changes when these data are changed.

nodes.name: the hyperbolic length $\mathcal{L}_{m,n}$
nodes.statement: We now prove that for $k=k_{m,n}$ the elastica is closed with hyperbolic length $$ \mathcal{L}_{m,n}:=2n\sqrt{2-k_{m,n}^2}K(k_{m,n}). $$

nodes.name: number of selfintersections of a closed elastica
nodes.statement: Such a selfintersection occurs if there are $s,t$ with $0\leq s<t<\mathcal{L}_{m,n}$ and $\gamma_{m,n}(s)=\gamma_{m,n}(t)$. The number of $s$, for which such $t\in (s,\mathcal{L}_{m,n})$ exist, is defined as the number of selfintersections.

nodes.name: the Willmore energy $\mathcal{W}_{m,n}$ of $\Sigma_{\gamma_{m,n}}$
nodes.statement: the Willmore energy \begin{align*} \mathcal{W}_{m,n} := \mathcal{W}(\Sigma_{\gamma_{m,n}}) = \frac{\pi}{2} \int_0^{\mathcal{L}_{m,n}} \kappa^2 \,ds = \frac{4n\pi E(k_{m,n})}{\sqrt{2-k_{m,n}^2}}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{W}_{m,n}=\frac{\pi}{2}\int_0^{\mathcal{L}_{m,n}}\kappa^2\,ds$, which evaluates to $4n\pi E(k_{m,n})/\sqrt{2-k_{m,n}^2}$.

nodes.name: the second variation functional $I_{m,n}$
nodes.statement: As pointed out by Langer and Singer (see equation (1.4) in \cite{LanSing_the_total}) the stability of $\gamma_{m,n}$ is determined by the integral $$ I_{m,n}(\phi) := \int_0^{\mathcal{L}_{m,n}} 2\phi''(s)^2-(5\kappa(s)^2-4)\phi'(s)^2+ (6\kappa'(s)^2-\kappa(s)^4+3\kappa(s)^2 + 2)\phi(s)^2 \,ds. $$ The functional $I_{m,n}$ measures the second variation of the Willmore energy $\mathcal{W}$ in direction $\phi N$ where $N$ is the normal vector field associated with $\gamma_{m,n}$ and $\phi$ is assumed to be $\mathcal{L}_{m,n}$-periodic and smooth.
nodes.statement_short: $I_{m,n}(\phi)$ is the second variation of the Willmore energy in the normal direction $\phi N$.
nodes.origin_citation: Langer & Singer, the total squared curvature, eq. (1.4)
nodes.genus: second variation of the Willmore energy $\mathcal{W}$

nodes.name: stable / unstable elastica
nodes.statement: The elastica $\gamma_{m,n}$ is said to be stable if the above functional is nonnegative, otherwise we will say that it is unstable.

nodes.name: Hausdorff convergence of surfaces in $(\Hh,d_{\Hh})$
nodes.statement: We will use the notion of Hausdorff convergence defined by $\Sigma_n\to\Sigma$ in the Hausdorff sense if and only if $d_H(\Sigma_n,\Sigma)\to 0$ as $n\to\infty$ where $$ d_H(\Sigma',\Sigma) = \max \big\{ \sup_{z'\in\Sigma'}\inf_{z\in\Sigma} d_{\Hh}(z',z), \sup_{z\in\Sigma}\inf_{z'\in\Sigma'} d_{\Hh}(z',z)\big\} $$ and $\Sigma,\Sigma',\Sigma_n$ are subsets of the (metric) hyperbolic space $(\Hh,d_{\Hh})$.

nodes.name: the functions $W_j,\hat W_j$ (wavelike case)
nodes.statement: Similarly to the orbitlike case we define \begin{align} W_j(s) := \frac{1}{\sqrt{2k^2-1}}w_j\big( \frac{s+s_*}{\sqrt{2k^2-1}}\big),\quad \hat W_j(s) := \frac{2k}{2k^2-1} \hat w_j\big( \frac{s+s_*}{\sqrt{2k^2-1}}\big). \qquad (j=1,2) \end{align} Notice that Part (v) of the previous proposition ensures that $W_1,W_2$ are well-defined and smooth on $\R\sm\{\kappa=0\}$ whereas $\hat W_1,\hat W_2$ are well-defined and smooth on $\R$ with $\hat W_j(s)=\kappa(s)W_j(s)$ whenever $\kappa(s)\neq 0$. The exact formulas for $\hat w_1,\hat w_2$ show that $\hat W_1,\hat W_2$ look like shifted and rescaled versions of $-\sinh$ and $\cosh$.
nodes.statement_short: $W_j$ and the smoothed $\hat W_j=\kappa W_j$ rescale $w_j,\hat w_j$; the $\hat W_j$ are smooth on all of $\R$.

nodes.name: the angle function $\vartheta$ (wavelike case)
nodes.statement: By Proposition~\ref{prop:W1W2_wavelike}~(i) and~\eqref{eq:def_Wj_wavelike} there is a smooth function $\vartheta$ such that \begin{align} \hat W_2(s)-i\hat W_1(s) = \sqrt{\kappa(s)^2-\mu} \big( \cosh(\vartheta(s))+i \sinh(\vartheta(s)) \big). \end{align} Again $\vartheta$ is thus defined only up to additive multiples of $2\pi$ so that we may require $\vartheta$ to satisfy the inequality $-2\pi<\vartheta(-s_*)\leq 0$.
nodes.statement_short: In the wavelike case $\vartheta$ is the hyperbolic angle of $\hat W_2-i\hat W_1$.

nodes.name: the shorthands $\sigma_1,\sigma_2,\sigma_3,\sigma_4$
nodes.statement: It is convenient to use the following shorthand notations: \begin{align} \begin{aligned} &\sigma_1 := \frac{1-\mu(a_3^2A_2^2+(a_3A_1-b_3)^2)}{2A_2a_3}, &&\sigma_2:= \sqrt\mu (A_1a_3-b_3),\\ &\sigma_3 := \frac{1-\mu(a_3^2B_2^2+(a_3B_1-b_3)^2)}{2B_2a_3}, &&\sigma_4:=\sqrt\mu (B_1a_3-b_3). \end{aligned} \end{align}

nodes.name: the Halphen-Hermite solutions $w_+,w_-$
nodes.statement: From \cite{Whit_modern_analysis}, p.570--575 we obtain that every solution of $w''+2\dn^2(\cdot,k)w=0$ is a linear combination of the so-called Halphen-Hermite solutions $w_+,w_-:\R\to\C$ (first discovered in \cite{Her_extrait,Hal_fonc_ell}) which are given by \begin{equation} w_\pm(s) = \frac{H(s\mp i\alpha,k)}{\Theta(s,k)}e^{s\zeta(\pm i\alpha,k)}\quad\text{for } \alpha\in\C \text{ s.t.} \dn^2(i\alpha,k)=2-k^2. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Every solution of the Lam\'e equation $w''+2\dn^2 w=0$ is a combination of the Halphen-Hermite solutions $w_\pm=H(s\mp i\alpha)/\Theta(s)\,e^{s\zeta(\pm i\alpha)}$.
nodes.origin_citation: Hermite; Halphen; Whittaker, Modern Analysis p.570-575

nodes.name: the parameter $\alpha_k$ (orbitlike case)
nodes.statement: so that one possible choice is $\alpha=\alpha_k$ where $\sn(\alpha_k,k')=k'$, i.e. $\alpha_k:=F(k',k')$, see \eqref{eq:Jac_Inverse}.

nodes.name: the fundamental system $w_1,w_2$ (orbitlike case)
nodes.statement: We then define $w_1,w_2:\R\to\R$ through the formula \begin{equation} w_1(s)+iw_2(s) := \frac{\sqrt{1-k^2}}{\Im(w_+(0))} w_+(s) \end{equation} so that (i) holds.

nodes.name: the functions $w_\pm$ and $\alpha_k$ (wavelike case)
nodes.statement: The proof is similar to the orbitlike case. We define $$ w_\pm (s) := \frac{\Theta_1(s\pm\alpha_k,k)}{\Theta(s,k)} e^{\mp s\zeta(\alpha_k,k)} \quad\text{where }\dn^2(\alpha_k,k)=k^2, \text{ i.e. }\alpha_k:= F(k'/k,k) $$ for $\Theta,\Theta_1,\zeta$ as in section~\ref{sec:Jacobi}.

nodes.name: the fundamental system $w_1,w_2$ (wavelike case)
the smooth extensions $\hat w_1,\hat w_2$ (wavelike case)
nodes.statement: Finally, \eqref{eq:defn_w1w2_wavelike} shows that property (v) holds for the choice \begin{align*} \hat w_1(s) &:= \frac{k(w_+(s) - w_-(s))}{w_+(0)+w_-(0)} =\frac{k(\Theta_1(s+\alpha_k,k)e^{-s\zeta(\alpha_k,k)} - \Theta_1(s-\alpha_k,k)e^{s\zeta(\alpha_k,k)}}{ (w_+(0)+w_-(0))\Theta(s,k)}, \\ \hat w_2(s) &:= \frac{k(w_+(s) + w_-(s))}{w_+(0)+w_-(0)} = \frac{k(\Theta_1(s+\alpha_k,k)e^{-s\zeta(\alpha_k,k)} + \Theta_1(s-\alpha_k,k)e^{s\zeta(\alpha_k,k)}}{ (w_+(0)+w_-(0))\Theta(s,k)}, \end{align*}

nodes.name: standing hypothesis: $\gamma$ is an orbitlike elastica with curvature $\kappa$
nodes.statement: So from now on let always $\gamma:\R\to\Hh$ denote an orbitlike elastica with (hyperbolic) curvature function \begin{equation} \kappa(s)=\frac{2}{\sqrt{2-k^2}}\dn(\frac{s+s_*}{\sqrt{2-k^2}},k) \end{equation} for $0<k<1,s_*\in\R$ and let $\phi,Z$ be defined as in \eqref{eq:ODE_solution},\eqref{eq:def_Z}. We recall $\mu= 4(1-k^2)/(2-k^2)^2$.
nodes.statement_short: Throughout section 5, $\gamma$ is an orbitlike elastica with $\kappa(s)=\frac{2}{\sqrt{2-k^2}}\dn(\frac{s+s_*}{\sqrt{2-k^2}},k)$ and $\mu=4(1-k^2)/(2-k^2)^2$.

nodes.name: standing hypothesis: $\gamma$ is a wavelike elastica with curvature $\kappa$
nodes.statement: In this section we consider wavelike elasticae associated with curvature functions \begin{equation} \kappa(s) = \frac{2k}{\sqrt{2k^2-1}} \cn\Big( \frac{s+s_*}{\sqrt{2k^2-1}},k\Big),\qquad\text{where } \frac{1}{\sqrt 2}<k<1,\;s_*\in\R. \end{equation} The functions $\phi$ and $Z(\cdot,P)$ are defined as before and we set $$ \mu:= -(\kappa')^2+\kappa^2-\frac{1}{4}\kappa^4 = -\frac{4k^2(1-k^2)}{(2k^2-1)^2}. $$
nodes.statement_short: Throughout section 6, $\kappa(s)=\frac{2k}{\sqrt{2k^2-1}}\cn(\frac{s+s_*}{\sqrt{2k^2-1}},k)$ with $\tfrac1{\sqrt2}<k<1$, so $\mu<0$.

nodes.name: positively oriented orbitlike elastica in the Dirichlet problem
nodes.statement: In this section we investigate the Dirichlet problem for orbitlike elasticae. As in our previous considerations we assume the elastica to be positively oriented so that its curvature function is positive and given by \eqref{eq:def_kappa_orbitlike}.

nodes.name: the Willmore equation
nodes.statement: The Willmore equation $$ -\Delta_\Sigma H = 2H(H^2-K) $$ for such graphical surfaces of revolution then simplifies to a rather complicated nonlinear ODE of fourth order for the profile function (see for instance (2.5) in \cite{DalAcFroGruSch_Symmetric}) coming with appropriate boundary conditions.
nodes.statement_short: The Euler-Lagrange equation $-\Delta_\Sigma H=2H(H^2-K)$ of the Willmore functional.
nodes.origin_citation: classical Willmore equation; cf. (2.5) in Dall'Acqua, Fr\"ohlich, Grunau & Schieweck

nodes.name: the ODE system recovering $\gamma$ from its curvature
nodes.statement: So, a curve $\gamma$ may be recovered from its curvature function $\kappa$ by solving the ODE system \begin{align} \gamma_1' = \gamma_2 \cos(\phi),\quad \gamma_2' = \gamma_2 \sin(\phi),\quad \phi' + \cos(\phi) = \kappa. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: $\gamma_1'=\gamma_2\cos\phi,\ \gamma_2'=\gamma_2\sin\phi,\ \phi'+\cos\phi=\kappa$.

nodes.name: the curvature ODE of elasticae and the invariant $\mu$
nodes.statement: From section 2 in \cite{LanSing_the_total} we get that $\kappa$ satisfies \begin{equation} -\kappa''+\kappa =\frac{1}{2}\kappa^3,\qquad\quad \mu := -(\kappa')^2+ \kappa^2 - \frac{1}{4}\kappa^4 \in\R. \end{equation}
nodes.statement_short: Elastica curvature satisfies $-\kappa''+\kappa=\tfrac12\kappa^3$ with conserved quantity $\mu$.

nodes.origin_citation: Langer & Singer, the total squared curvature, section 2

nodes.name: derivatives of the complete elliptic integrals $K,E$
nodes.statement: The derivatives of these functions are known to be (see 710.00 and 710.02 in \cite{ByrFri_handbook}) \begin{align} K'(k) = \frac{E(k)-(1-k^2)K(k)}{k(1-k^2)},\qquad E'(k) = \frac{E(k)-K(k)}{k}. \end{align}

nodes.name: the Jacobi trigonometric identities
nodes.statement: Thanks to the identities \begin{align} \cn^2+\sn^2 = 1,\qquad \dn^2+k^2\sn^2 = 1, \end{align} these functions are globally defined and satisfy

nodes.statement: Differentiating $Z$ gives the formula \begin{equation} Z' = \frac{\gamma_1-P_1}{P_2} \cdot \cos(\phi) + \frac{\gamma_2^2-P_2^2-(\gamma_1-P_1)^2}{2P_2\gamma_2}\cdot \sin(\phi). \end{equation}

nodes.name: definition of the angle function $\phi$ from the coefficients (orbitlike)
nodes.statement: Motivated by the formulas~\eqref{eq:b3a3_1},\eqref{eq:b3a3_2} derived in the ''only if''-part we define $\phi$ via \begin{equation} \vecII{\sin(\phi)}{\cos(\phi)} := \frac{\mu a_3}{2(\kappa^2-\mu)}\matII{\kappa^2}{2\kappa'}{2\kappa'}{-\kappa^2} \vecII{\gamma_1-\frac{b_3}{a_3}}{\gamma_2-\frac{\kappa}{\mu a_3}}. \end{equation}

nodes.name: Jacobi's imaginary transformation applied to $\dn(i\alpha,k)^2$
nodes.statement: By Jacobi's imaginary transformation (see 161.01 in \cite{ByrFri_handbook}) we have $$ \dn(i\alpha,k)^2 = \frac{\dn^2(\alpha,k')}{\cn^2(\alpha,k')} \stackrel{\eqref{eq:Jacobi_trigonometric_identities}}{=} \frac{1-(k')^2\sn^2(\alpha,k')}{1-\sn^2(\alpha,k')} = 1 + \frac{k^2\sn^2(\alpha,k')}{1-\sn^2(\alpha,k')} \qquad (k':=\sqrt{1-k^2})

nodes.name: the substitution $z=-K(k)+(s+s_*)/\sqrt{2-k^2}$ and the resulting formulas
nodes.statement: For the proof we set $z:=-K(k)+ \frac{s+s_*}{\sqrt{2-k^2}}$ so that \eqref{eq:def_kappa_orbitlike},\eqref{eq:def_Wj} give \begin{align} \begin{aligned} w_j(z)= \sqrt{2-k^2}W_j(s),&\quad w_j'(z)= (2-k^2)W_j'(s) \quad (j=1,2)\\ \kappa(s) &= \frac{2}{\sqrt{2-k^2}}\dn(z+K(k),k),\\ \kappa'(s) &= -\frac{2k^2}{2-k^2}\sn(z+K(k),k)\cn(z+K(k),k). \end{aligned} \end{align}

nodes.name: $\dn(z,k)$ and $\sn(z,k)\cn(z,k)$ in terms of $\kappa,\kappa'$
nodes.statement: Using the identities from \eqref{eq:Jac_Additionstheoreme} we get \begin{align} \begin{aligned} \dn(z,k) &= \frac{\sqrt{1-k^2}}{\dn(z+K(k),k)} \stackrel{\eqref{eq:formulas_z_vs_s}}{=} \frac{2\sqrt{1-k^2}}{\sqrt{2-k^2}} \frac{1}{\kappa(s)}, \\ \sn(z,k)\cn(z,k) &= - \frac{\sqrt{1-k^2} \sn(z+K(k),k)\cn(z+K(k),k)}{\dn^2(z+K(k),k)} \stackrel{\eqref{eq:formulas_z_vs_s}}{=} \frac{2\sqrt{1-k^2}}{k^2} \frac{\kappa'(s)}{\kappa(s)^2}. \end{aligned} \end{align}

nodes.name: Langer-Singer classification of closed elasticae in $\Hh$
nodes.statement: Let $\gamma$ be a regular closed curve in $\Hh$ which is critical for the elastic energy functional. Then either $\gamma$ is the $m$-fold cover of the ball for some $m$, or $\gamma$ is a member of the family of solutions $\gamma_{m,n}$ having the following description: if $m>1$ and $n$ are integers satisfying $1<\frac{2m}{n}<\sqrt{2}$ there is (up to congruence) a unique curve $\gamma_{m,n}$, which closes up in $n$ periods of its curvature $\kappa=\kappa_0 \cn^2(rs,p)$ while making $m$ orbits about the fixed point of the associated rotation field $J$. Further, $\gamma_{m,n}$ oscillates between a pair of invariant circles of $J$ with the $n$ maxima of $\kappa$ equally spaced around the outer circle and the $n$ minima of $\kappa$ equally spaced around the inner circle. Also, $\gamma_{m,n}$ has $n(m-1)$ points of selfintersections.
nodes.statement_short: Every closed elastica in $\Hh$ is either an $m$-fold covered circle or one of the curves $\gamma_{m,n}$ with $1<2m/n<\sqrt2$, which oscillates between two invariant circles and has $n(m-1)$ selfintersections.
nodes.origin_citation: Langer & Singer, Curves in the hyperbolic plane, Theorem 3
assumptions: Let $\gamma$ be a regular closed curve in $\Hh$ which is critical for the elastic energy functional.
conclusions: either $\gamma$ is the $m$-fold cover of the ball for some $m$, or $\gamma$ is a member of the family of solutions $\gamma_{m,n}$ having the following description

nodes.name: Symmetry of orbitlike solutions of the symmetric Dirichlet problem
nodes.statement: Assume $A_1=-B_1\neq 0, A_2=B_2>0,\phi_A+\phi_B\in 2\pi\Z$ such that $$ \pm\big(\frac{A_2}{A_1}\sin(\phi_A) + \cos(\phi_A)\big) \notin (0,2). $$ Then all positively $(\pm=+)$ respectively negatively $(\pm=-)$ oriented orbitlike solutions of~\eqref{eq:DirichletBVP} are symmetric.
nodes.statement_short: Under symmetric boundary data with $\pm(\tfrac{A_2}{A_1}\sin\phi_A+\cos\phi_A)\notin(0,2)$, every orbitlike solution of the Dirichlet problem is symmetric.
conclusions: Then all positively $(\pm=+)$ respectively negatively $(\pm=-)$ oriented orbitlike solutions of~\eqref{eq:DirichletBVP} are symmetric.

nodes.name: Symmetry breaking for the Willmore Dirichlet problem
nodes.statement: There are boundary data $A_1=-B_1,A_2=B_2>0,\phi_A=-\phi_B$ such that \eqref{eq:DirichletBVP} has uncountably many nonsymmetric solutions.
nodes.statement_short: There exist symmetric Dirichlet data admitting uncountably many nonsymmetric Willmore solutions.
conclusions: There are boundary data $A_1=-B_1,A_2=B_2>0,\phi_A=-\phi_B$ such that \eqref{eq:DirichletBVP} has uncountably many nonsymmetric solutions.

nodes.name: Explicit formulas for orbitlike elasticae
nodes.statement: A curve $\gamma:\R\to \Hh$ is an orbitlike elastica parametrized by hyperbolic arclength if and only if we have \begin{align} \gamma_1(s) &=\frac{b_1 W_1(s)+b_2 W_2(s)+b_3}{a_1 W_1(s)+a_2 W_2(s)+a_3}, \\ \gamma_2(s) &=\frac{1}{\kappa(s)(a_1 W_1(s)+a_2 W_2(s)+a_3)} \end{align} for $a_1,a_2,a_3,b_1,b_2,b_3\in\R$ such that \begin{equation} a_3= \sqrt{a_1^2+a_2^2}>0,\qquad \vecII{b_1}{b_2} = \frac{b_3}{a_3} \vecII{a_1}{a_2} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu}a_3} \vecII{-a_2}{a_1}. \end{equation} In this case we moreover have for all $s\in\R$ \begin{align} \gamma_2(s)(a_1,a_2)^T&= \xi^1(s) , \\ \gamma_2(s) (b_1,b_2)^T &= \gamma_1(s) \xi^1(s)+ \gamma_2(s) \xi^3(s), \\ \gamma_1(s) &= \frac{b_3}{a_3} +\frac{1}{2\mu a_3}\big(\kappa(s)^2\sin(\phi(s))+2\kappa'(s)\cos(\phi(s))\big), \\ \gamma_2(s) &= \frac{\kappa(s)}{\mu a_3} + \frac{1}{2\mu a_3}\big(2\kappa'(s)\sin(\phi(s))-\kappa(s)^2\cos(\phi(s))\big). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Orbitlike elasticae are exactly the M\"obius-type quotients $\gamma_1=(b_1W_1+b_2W_2+b_3)/(a_1W_1+a_2W_2+a_3)$, $\gamma_2=1/(\kappa(a_1W_1+a_2W_2+a_3))$ with $a_3=\sqrt{a_1^2+a_2^2}>0$.

nodes.name: Explicit formulas for wavelike elasticae
nodes.statement: A curve $\gamma:\R\to \Hh$ is a wavelike elastica parametrized by hyperbolic arclength if and only if we have \begin{align} \begin{aligned} \gamma_1(s) &=\frac{b_1 \hat W_1(s)+b_2 \hat W_2(s)+b_3 \kappa(s)}{a_1 \hat W_1(s)+a_2 \hat W_2(s)+a_3\kappa(s)}, \\ \gamma_2(s) &=\frac{1}{a_1 \hat W_1(s)+a_2\hat W_2(s) + a_3\kappa(s)}. \end{aligned} \end{align} for $a_1,a_2,a_3,b_1,b_2,b_3\in\R$ such that \begin{align} \begin{aligned} &\text{either}\qquad a_3\neq 0, \;\; a_2=\sqrt{a_1^2+a_3^2},\; \; \vecII{b_1}{b_2} = \frac{b_3}{a_3} \vecII{a_1}{a_2} - \frac{1}{\sqrt{|\mu|}a_3} \vecII{a_2}{a_1} \\ &\text{or }\qquad\quad\, a_3=0,\;\; a_2=|a_1|,\;\; b_1=\sign(a_1)b_2,\;\; |b_3| = \frac{1}{\sqrt{|\mu|}}. \end{aligned} \end{align} In this case the identities \eqref{eq:a1a2b1b2_1},\eqref{eq:a1a2b1b2_2} hold on $\R\sm\{\kappa=0\}$ and for all $s\in\R$ we have \begin{align} a_3\gamma_1(s) &= b_3 +\frac{1}{2\mu}\big(\kappa(s)^2\sin(\phi(s))+2\kappa'(s)\cos(\phi(s))\big), \\ a_3\gamma_2(s) &= \frac{\kappa(s)}{\mu} + \frac{1}{2\mu}\big(2\kappa'(s)\sin(\phi(s))-\kappa(s)^2\cos(\phi(s))\big). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Wavelike elasticae are exactly the quotients built from $\hat W_1,\hat W_2,\kappa$ subject to either $a_3\neq0,\,a_2=\sqrt{a_1^2+a_3^2}$ or the degenerate branch $a_3=0$.

conclusions: \gamma_1(s) &=\frac{b_1 \hat W_1(s)+b_2 \hat W_2(s)+b_3 \kappa(s)}{a_1 \hat W_1(s)+a_2 \hat W_2(s)+a_3\kappa(s)}, \\ \gamma_2(s) &=\frac{1}{a_1 \hat W_1(s)+a_2\hat W_2(s) + a_3\kappa(s)}.

nodes.name: Existence and possible non-uniqueness of graphical solutions of the Dirichlet problem
nodes.statement: One example for a result in the graphical setting can be found in the papers \cite{DalAcDecGru_Classical_solutions,DalAcFroGruSch_Symmetric}: For $A_1=-B_1,A_2=B_2$ and $\phi_A=-\phi_B \in [0,\pi/2)$ the Dirichlet problem has a graphical solution which, by Theorem~1.1 in \cite{Eich_nonuniqueness}, may in general fail to be unique.
nodes.statement_short: For $A_1=-B_1,A_2=B_2,\phi_A=-\phi_B\in[0,\pi/2)$ a graphical solution exists but need not be unique.
nodes.origin_citation: Dall'Acqua, Deckelnick & Grunau; Dall'Acqua, Fr\"ohlich, Grunau & Schieweck; Eichmann (nonuniqueness) Thm 1.1
conclusions: the Dirichlet problem has a graphical solution which, by Theorem~1.1 in \cite{Eich_nonuniqueness}, may in general fail to be unique.

nodes.name: Symmetry of the graphical least energy solution (Koeller and Eichmann)
nodes.statement: They were able to prove the symmetry of one particular solution of this boundary value problem, namely of the graphical least energy solution. Indeed, the energy of this solution is smaller than $4\pi$ according to Theorem~1.1 in \cite{DalAcDecGru_Classical_solutions} whereas nonsymmetric solutions (if they exist) have Willmore-energy $>4\pi$ by Theorem~3.9 in \cite{Eich_symmetry}.
nodes.statement_short: The graphical least-energy solution of the symmetric problem is symmetric, its energy being $<4\pi$ while nonsymmetric solutions would have energy $>4\pi$.
nodes.origin_citation: Eichmann (symmetry) Thm 1.1 and Thm 3.9; Dall'Acqua, Deckelnick & Grunau Thm 1.1
conclusions: They were able to prove the symmetry of one particular solution of this boundary value problem, namely of the graphical least energy solution.

nodes.name: Gap theorem of Mondino and Nguyen
nodes.statement: By a gap theorem due to Mondino and Nguyen \cite{MonNgu_gap_theorem} one knows that the Clifford torus can not be approximated by Willmore tori with respect to the Willmore energy functional. As a consequence it may only be approximated in a weaker sense.
nodes.statement_short: The Clifford torus is isolated in the Willmore energy: no sequence of Willmore tori approximates it energetically.
conclusions: the Clifford torus can not be approximated by Willmore tori with respect to the Willmore energy functional

nodes.name: Instability criterion for $\gamma_{m,n}$
nodes.statement: The curve $\gamma_{m,n}$ is unstable provided \begin{align*} n > \frac{A(k_{m,n})+\sqrt{A(k_{m,n})^2+4B(k_{m,n})C(k_{m,n})}}{2C(k_{m,n})} \end{align*} where \begin{align*} A(k) &:= \frac{\pi\sqrt{5E(k)-(2-k^2)K(k)}}{(2-k^2)K(k)^{3/2}},\\ B(k) &:= \frac{\pi^2}{(2-k^2)K(k)^2}, \\ C(k) &:= \frac{\sqrt{(16(1-k^2)K(k)^2-44(2-k^2)E(k)K(k)+75E(k)^2)_+}}{\sqrt{3}(2-k^2)K(k)}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: A monochromatic test function shows $\gamma_{m,n}$ is unstable once $n$ exceeds an explicit root of $A/n+B/n^2=C$.

nodes.name: Hausdorff approximation of the Clifford torus by $\Sigma_{\gamma_{m_n,n}}$
nodes.statement: Let $(m_n)$ be a sequence such that $1<2m_n/n<\sqrt 2$ for all $n\in\N$. Then, as $n\to\infty$, the sequence $(\Sigma_{\gamma_{m_n,n}})$ diverges with respect to the Willmore energy and it converges (up to M\"obius transformations) to the Clifford torus in the Hausdorff sense if and only if $2m_n/n\to \sqrt{2}$. In this case, almost all of the Willmore surfaces are unstable.
nodes.statement_short: $\Sigma_{\gamma_{m_n,n}}$ converges to the Clifford torus in the Hausdorff sense exactly when $2m_n/n\to\sqrt2$, while its Willmore energy always diverges.
assumptions: Let $(m_n)$ be a sequence such that $1<2m_n/n<\sqrt 2$ for all $n\in\N$.
conclusions: Then, as $n\to\infty$, the sequence $(\Sigma_{\gamma_{m_n,n}})$ diverges with respect to the Willmore energy and it converges (up to M\"obius transformations) to the Clifford torus in the Hausdorff sense if and only if $2m_n/n\to \sqrt{2}$.
In this case, almost all of the Willmore surfaces are unstable.

nodes.name: Second order ODE satisfied by the conformal invariant $Z(\cdot;P)$
nodes.statement: Let $\gamma:\R\to\Hh$ be parametrized by hyperbolic arclength and $Z$ be given by \eqref{eq:def_Z}. Then, for all $P\in \C^2$ with $P_2\neq 0$, the function $Z(\cdot;P)$ satisfies \begin{equation} \kappa Z''-2\kappa'Z'+\kappa(Z+1)\equiv 2\mu C \end{equation} where $C\in\C$ is, for any $s_0\in\R$, given by \begin{align} \begin{aligned} C &= \frac{P_2^2+(\gamma_1(s_0)-P_1)^2}{2P_2\gamma_2(s_0)}\cdot\Big(\frac{\kappa(s_0)}{\mu}+\frac{\kappa'(s_0)}{\mu}\sin(\phi(s_0)) - \frac{\kappa(s_0)^2}{2\mu}\cos(\phi(s_0))\Big) \\ & + \frac{\gamma_2(s_0)}{2P_2}\cdot \Big(\frac{\kappa(s_0)}{\mu}-\frac{\kappa'(s_0)}{\mu}\sin(\phi(s_0)) + \frac{\kappa(s_0)^2}{2\mu}\cos(\phi(s_0))\Big) \\ &+ \frac{\gamma_1(s_0)-P_1}{P_2}\cdot \Big( -\frac{\kappa(s_0)^2}{2\mu}\sin(\phi(s_0))-\frac{\kappa'(s_0)}{\mu}\cos(\phi(s_0)) \Big). \end{aligned} \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Along any arclength-parametrized curve, $\kappa Z''-2\kappa'Z'+\kappa(Z+1)$ is the constant $2\mu C$.

nodes.name: Fundamental system $\{w_1,w_2\}$ of the Lam\'e equation $w''+2\dn^2 w=0$
nodes.statement: For all $k\in (0,1)$ the ordinary differential equation $w''+2\dn^2(\cdot,k)w=0$ has a fundamental system $\{w_1,w_2\}$ on $\R$ such that the following holds: \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] $w_1$ is odd about 0, $w_2$ is even about 0, $w_2(0)>0>w_1'(0)$, \item[(ii)] $w_1(s)^2+w_2(s)^2=2-k^2 -\dn^2(s,k)$ on $\R$, \item[(iii)] $w_1(s)w_1'(s)+w_2(s)w_2'(s) = k^2\dn(s,k)\cn(s,k)\sn(s,k)$ on $\R$, \item[(iv)] $w_1(s)w_2'(s)-w_2(s)w_1'(s) = \sqrt{1-k^2}\sqrt{2-k^2}$ on $\R$, \item[(v)] $(w_1+iw_2)(s+2lK(k)) = (w_1+iw_2)(s) e^{il\Delta\theta_k}$ for all $s\in\R,l\in\Z$, \item[(vi)] $(w_1+iw_2)(-K(k)) = e^{i(\pi-\Delta\theta_k)/2}$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: The Lam\'e equation $w''+2\dn^2(\cdot,k)w=0$ has a real fundamental system with prescribed parity, a Pythagorean identity, constant Wronskian $\sqrt{(1-k^2)(2-k^2)}$ and quasi-periodicity factor $e^{i\Delta\theta_k}$.

nodes.name: Identities for the fundamental system $\{W_1,W_2\}$ (orbitlike)
nodes.statement: Let $\kappa$ be given by \eqref{eq:def_kappa_orbitlike}. Then $\{W_1,W_2\}$ is a fundamental system of the ODE $W''+2\mu\kappa^{-2}W=0$ and the following identities hold on $\R$: \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] $W_1^2+W_2^2 = \frac{\kappa^2-\mu}{\kappa^2}$, \item[(ii)] $W_1'= \frac{\mu \kappa'}{\kappa(\kappa^2-\mu)} W_1 - \frac{\sqrt\mu \kappa^2}{2(\kappa^2-\mu)}W_2 $, \item[(iii)] $W_2' = \frac{\sqrt\mu \kappa^2}{2(\kappa^2-\mu)}W_1 + \frac{\mu \kappa'}{\kappa(\kappa^2-\mu)} W_2$, \item[(iv)] $W_1W_2'-W_2W_1' = \frac{\sqrt{\mu}}{2}$, \item[(v)] $(W_1+iW_2)(s+2l\sqrt{2-k^2}K(k))=(W_1+iW_2)(s)e^{il\Delta\theta_k}$ for $s\in\R,l\in\Z$, \item[(vi)] $(W_1+iW_2)(s)= (-W_1+iW_2)(-s-2s_*+2l\sqrt{2-k^2}K(k)) e^{i(l-1)\Delta\theta_k}$ for $s\in\R,l\in\Z$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: $\{W_1,W_2\}$ solves $W''+2\mu\kappa^{-2}W=0$ and satisfies $W_1^2+W_2^2=(\kappa^2-\mu)/\kappa^2$, a linear first-order system, Wronskian $\sqrt\mu/2$ and two reflection/rotation identities.
conclusions: Then $\{W_1,W_2\}$ is a fundamental system of the ODE $W''+2\mu\kappa^{-2}W=0$ and the following identities hold on $\R$:

nodes.name: Properties of the angle function $\vartheta$ (orbitlike)
nodes.statement: The following identities hold: $$ \vartheta' = \frac{\sqrt\mu \kappa^2}{2(\kappa^2-\mu)},\qquad \matII{W_1}{W_2}{W_1'}{W_2'} = \matII{0}{\frac{\sqrt{\kappa^2-\mu}}{\kappa}}{\frac{-\sqrt{\mu}\kappa}{2\sqrt{\kappa^2-\mu}}}{ \frac{\mu\kappa'}{\kappa^2\sqrt{\kappa^2-\mu}}} \matII{\cos(\vartheta)}{\sin(\vartheta)}{-\sin(\vartheta)}{\cos(\vartheta)}. $$ Moreover, we have for $s\in\R,l\in\Z$ \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] $\vartheta(-s_*+l\sqrt{2-k^2}K(k)) = \frac{l-1}{2}\Delta\theta_k$, \item[(ii)] $\vartheta(s+2l\sqrt{2-k^2}K(k))-\vartheta(s) = l\Delta\theta_k$, \item[(iii)] $\vartheta(-s_*+s)+\vartheta(-s_*-s) = -\Delta\theta_k$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: $\vartheta'=\sqrt\mu\kappa^2/(2(\kappa^2-\mu))$, the matrix $(W_j,W_j')$ factors through a rotation $\mathcal{R}(\vartheta)$, and $\vartheta$ advances by $\Delta\theta_k$ per period.

nodes.name: Explicit formula for $Z(s;P)$ (orbitlike)
nodes.statement: For $P=(P_1,P_2)\in\R^2$ such that $P_2\neq 0$ we have \begin{equation} Z(s;P) = -1 + \kappa(s)\big( AW_1(s) + BW_2(s) + C\big) \end{equation} where $C$ is given by \eqref{eq:def_C} and $A,B\in\R$ satisfy \begin{align} \vecII{A}{B} &= \frac{(\gamma_1(s_0)-P_1)^2+P_2^2}{2\gamma_2(s_0)P_2} \xi^1(s_0) + \frac{\gamma_2(s_0)}{2P_2}\xi^2(s_0) + \frac{\gamma_1(s_0)-P_1}{P_2}\xi^3(s_0) \quad\forall s_0\in\R. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: $Z(s;P)=-1+\kappa(s)(AW_1(s)+BW_2(s)+C)$ with $(A,B)$ given by the $\xi^j(s_0)$ combination.
conclusions: where $C$ is given by \eqref{eq:def_C} and $A,B\in\R$ satisfy \begin{align} \vecII{A}{B} &= \frac{(\gamma_1(s_0)-P_1)^2+P_2^2}{2\gamma_2(s_0)P_2} \xi^1(s_0) + \frac{\gamma_2(s_0)}{2P_2}\xi^2(s_0) + \frac{\gamma_1(s_0)-P_1}{P_2}\xi^3(s_0) \quad\forall s_0\in\R.

nodes.name: The distinguished point $P$ with $A=B=0$ (orbitlike)
nodes.statement: For $P_1=\frac{b_3}{a_3},P_2=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu}a_3}$ we have for all $s\in\R$ $$ Z(s;P) = -1 + \frac{\kappa(s)}{\sqrt\mu}. $$
nodes.statement_short: At $P=(b_3/a_3,1/(\sqrt\mu a_3))$ the distance function collapses to $Z=-1+\kappa/\sqrt\mu$.

nodes.name: Orbitlike elasticae oscillate between two circles
nodes.statement: We have $\gamma(\R)\subset \overline{B_{R_1}(Q_1)}\sm B_{R_2}(Q_2)$ where \begin{align*} Q_1 &= \Big( \frac{b_3}{a_3},\frac{\sqrt{2+2\sqrt{1-\mu}}}{\mu a_3}\Big),\qquad R_1 = \frac{\sqrt{2-\mu+2\sqrt{1-\mu}}}{\mu a_3}, \\ Q_2 &= \Big( \frac{b_3}{a_3},\frac{\sqrt{2-2\sqrt{1-\mu}}}{\mu a_3}\Big),\qquad R_2 = \frac{\sqrt{2-\mu-2\sqrt{1-\mu}}}{\mu a_3}. \end{align*} The curve $\gamma$ touches $\partial B_{R_1}(Q_1)$ exactly when $\kappa$ attains its maximum and it touches $\partial B_{R_2}(Q_2)$ precisely when $\kappa$ attains its minimum.
nodes.statement_short: Every orbitlike elastica lies in the annulus $\overline{B_{R_1}(Q_1)}\setminus B_{R_2}(Q_2)$, touching the outer/inner circle at the maxima/minima of $\kappa$.
conclusions: Q_1 &= \Big( \frac{b_3}{a_3},\frac{\sqrt{2+2\sqrt{1-\mu}}}{\mu a_3}\Big),\qquad R_1 = \frac{\sqrt{2-\mu+2\sqrt{1-\mu}}}{\mu a_3}, \\ Q_2 &= \Big( \frac{b_3}{a_3},\frac{\sqrt{2-2\sqrt{1-\mu}}}{\mu a_3}\Big),\qquad R_2 = \frac{\sqrt{2-\mu-2\sqrt{1-\mu}}}{\mu a_3}.
The curve $\gamma$ touches $\partial B_{R_1}(Q_1)$ exactly when $\kappa$ attains its maximum and it touches $\partial B_{R_2}(Q_2)$ precisely when $\kappa$ attains its minimum.

nodes.name: Monotonicity of $k\mapsto \Delta\theta_k$
nodes.statement: The function $k\mapsto \Delta\theta_k$ decreases on $(0,1)$ from its upper limit $\sqrt{2}\pi$ to its lower limit $\pi$.
nodes.statement_short: $\Delta\theta_k$ decreases from $\sqrt2\pi$ to $\pi$ as $k$ runs through $(0,1)$.
nodes.origin_citation: Langer & Singer, the total squared curvature, Proposition 5.3
conclusions: The function $k\mapsto \Delta\theta_k$ decreases on $(0,1)$ from its upper limit $\sqrt{2}\pi$ to its lower limit $\pi$.

nodes.name: Characterization of closed orbitlike elasticae and their winding number
nodes.statement: The elastica $\gamma$ is closed if and only if $k=k_{m,n}$ for (w.l.o.g.) coprime integers $m,n\in\N$. In this case $\gamma=\gamma_{m,n}$ closes up after $n$ periods of its curvature function and its winding number around $(P_1,P_2)=(\frac{b_3}{a_3},\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu}a_3})$ is $m$.
nodes.statement_short: An orbitlike elastica closes up iff $k=k_{m,n}$ for coprime $m,n$; it then closes after $n$ curvature periods with winding number $m$.
conclusions: The elastica $\gamma$ is closed if and only if $k=k_{m,n}$ for (w.l.o.g.) coprime integers $m,n\in\N$.
In this case $\gamma=\gamma_{m,n}$ closes up after $n$ periods of its curvature function and its winding number around $(P_1,P_2)=(\frac{b_3}{a_3},\frac{1}{\sqrt{\mu}a_3})$ is $m$.

nodes.name: The number of selfintersections of $\gamma_{m,n}$ is $n(m-1)$
nodes.statement: Let $m,n\in \N$ be coprime such that $1<\frac{2m}{n}<\sqrt 2$. Then the closed orbitlike elastica $\gamma_{m,n}$ has precisely $n(m-1)$ points of selfintersection characterized by the unique solutions $0\leq s<\mathcal{L}_{m,n}$ of the $n(m-1)$ equations \begin{equation} \frac{\vartheta(s)}{\pi} =\frac{(l-1)m}{n}-p \end{equation} where $l,p\in\Z$ satisfy the following conditions: \begin{align} \begin{aligned} l\in\{1,\ldots,2n-1\},\qquad p\in \big\{1,\ldots, \Big\lceil \frac{\min\{l,2n-l\}m}{n}\Big\rceil -1 \big\}. \end{aligned} \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: $\gamma_{m,n}$ has exactly $n(m-1)$ selfintersections, given by the solutions of $\vartheta(s)/\pi=(l-1)m/n-p$ over an explicit index range.
assumptions: where $l,p\in\Z$ satisfy the following conditions: \begin{align} \begin{aligned} l\in\{1,\ldots,2n-1\},\qquad p\in \big\{1,\ldots, \Big\lceil \frac{\min\{l,2n-l\}m}{n}\Big\rceil -1 \big\}.
conclusions: Then the closed orbitlike elastica $\gamma_{m,n}$ has precisely $n(m-1)$ points of selfintersection characterized by the unique solutions $0\leq s<\mathcal{L}_{m,n}$ of the $n(m-1)$ equations

nodes.name: Fundamental system $\{w_1,w_2\}$ of $w''-2(1-k^2)\cn^{-2}w=0$
nodes.statement: For all $k\in (0,1)$ the ordinary differential equation $w''- \frac{2(1-k^2)}{\cn^2(s,k)}w=0$ has a fundamental system $\{w_1,w_2\}$ on $(-K(k),K(k))$ such that the following holds: \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] $w_1$ is odd about 0, $w_2$ is even about 0, $w_2(0)>0>w_1'(0)$, \item[(ii)] $\cn^2(s,k)(w_2(s)^2 - w_1(s)^2) = 1-k^2+(2k^2-1)\cn^2(s,k)$ on $(-K(k),K(k))$, \item[(iii)] $\cn^3(s,k)(w_2(s)w_2'(s) - w_1(s)w_1'(s)) = (1-k^2)\sn(s,k)\dn(s,k)$ on $(-K(k),K(k))$, \item[(iv)] $w_2(s)w_1'(s)-w_1(s)w_2'(s)= -k\sqrt{(1-k^2)(2k^2-1)}$ on $(-K(k),K(k))$, \item[(v)] The functions $\cn(\cdot,k)w_1,\cn(\cdot,k)w_2$ have unique smooth extensions $\hat w_1,\hat w_2:\R\to\R$ such that the functions $w_1:=\frac{\hat w_1}{\cn(\cdot,k)},w_2:=\frac{\hat w_2}{\cn(\cdot,k)}$ build a fundamental system on each connected component of $\R\sm\{\kappa=0\}$. Moreover, $\hat w_2$ is positive on $\R$, $s\hat w_1(s)$ is negative on $\R\sm\{0\}$ and, as $s\to\pm\infty$, we have $\hat w_1(s)\to \mp\infty,\hat w_2(s)\to\infty$ exponentially and $\hat w_1(s)/\hat w_2(s)\to \mp 1$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: The wavelike Lam\'e-type equation has a fundamental system on $(-K,K)$ with prescribed parity, a hyperbolic Pythagorean identity, constant Wronskian and smooth extensions $\hat w_j=\cn\, w_j$ growing exponentially.
assumptions: For all $k\in (0,1)$ the ordinary differential equation $w''- \frac{2(1-k^2)}{\cn^2(s,k)}w=0$
conclusions: has a fundamental system $\{w_1,w_2\}$ on $(-K(k),K(k))$ such that the following holds:
$w_1$ is odd about 0, $w_2$ is even about 0, $w_2(0)>0>w_1'(0)$

The functions $\cn(\cdot,k)w_1,\cn(\cdot,k)w_2$ have unique smooth extensions $\hat w_1,\hat w_2:\R\to\R$ such that the functions $w_1:=\frac{\hat w_1}{\cn(\cdot,k)},w_2:=\frac{\hat w_2}{\cn(\cdot,k)}$ build a fundamental system on each connected component of $\R\sm\{\kappa=0\}$. Moreover, $\hat w_2$ is positive on $\R$, $s\hat w_1(s)$ is negative on $\R\sm\{0\}$ and, as $s\to\pm\infty$, we have $\hat w_1(s)\to \mp\infty,\hat w_2(s)\to\infty$ exponentially and $\hat w_1(s)/\hat w_2(s)\to \mp 1$

nodes.name: Identities for the fundamental system $\{W_1,W_2\}$ (wavelike)
nodes.statement: Let $\kappa$ be given by \eqref{eq:def_kappa_wavelike}. Then on each connected component of $\R\sm\{0\}$ the functions $W_1,W_2$ build a fundamental system of $W''+2\mu\kappa^{-2}W=0$ such that the following identities hold: \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] $W_2^2-W_1^2 = \frac{\kappa^2-\mu}{\kappa^2}$, \item[(ii)] $W_1'= \frac{\mu \kappa'}{\kappa(\kappa^2-\mu)} W_1 - \frac{\sqrt{|\mu|}\kappa^2}{2(\kappa^2-\mu)}W_2$, \item[(iii)] $W_2'= - \frac{\sqrt{|\mu|}\kappa^2}{2(\kappa^2-\mu)}W_1+ \frac{\mu \kappa'}{\kappa(\kappa^2-\mu)} W_2$, \item[(iv)] $W_2W_1'-W_1W_2' = - \frac{\sqrt{|\mu|}}{2}$. \end{itemize} Moreover, $\hat W_2$ is positive on $\R$ and we have $\hat W_1(s)/\hat W_2(s) \to \mp 1$ as $s\to\pm\infty$.
nodes.statement_short: In the wavelike case $W_2^2-W_1^2=(\kappa^2-\mu)/\kappa^2$, the pair solves a linear system with Wronskian $-\sqrt{|\mu|}/2$, and $\hat W_1/\hat W_2\to\mp1$.
conclusions: Then on each connected component of $\R\sm\{0\}$ the functions $W_1,W_2$ build a fundamental system of $W''+2\mu\kappa^{-2}W=0$ such that the following identities hold:
Moreover, $\hat W_2$ is positive on $\R$ and we have $\hat W_1(s)/\hat W_2(s) \to \mp 1$ as $s\to\pm\infty$.

nodes.name: Properties of the angle function $\vartheta$ (wavelike)
nodes.statement: For $W_1,W_2,\vartheta$ as above the following identities hold on $\R\sm\{\kappa=0\}$: $$ \vartheta' = \frac{\sqrt{|\mu|} \kappa^2}{2(\kappa^2-\mu)},\quad \matII{W_1}{W_2}{W_1'}{W_2'} = \matII{0}{\frac{\sqrt{\kappa^2-\mu}}{\kappa}}{-\frac{\sqrt{|\mu|}\kappa}{2\sqrt{\kappa^2-\mu}}}{ \frac{\mu\kappa'}{\kappa^2\sqrt{\kappa^2-\mu}}} \matII{\cosh(\vartheta)}{-\sinh(\vartheta)}{-\sinh(\vartheta)}{\cosh(\vartheta)}. $$
nodes.statement_short: In the wavelike case $\vartheta'=\sqrt{|\mu|}\kappa^2/(2(\kappa^2-\mu))$ and $(W_j,W_j')$ factors through a hyperbolic rotation $\mathcal{R}_h(\vartheta)$.

nodes.name: Explicit formula for $Z(s;P)$ (wavelike)
nodes.statement: For $P\in\C^2,P_2\neq 0$ we have \begin{equation} Z(s;P) = -1 + A \hat W_1(s) + B\hat W_2(s) + C\kappa(s) \end{equation} where $A,B,C\in\C$ are given by \eqref{eq:formula_AB},\eqref{eq:def_C} whenever $\kappa(s_0)\neq 0$.
nodes.statement_short: $Z(s;P)=-1+A\hat W_1(s)+B\hat W_2(s)+C\kappa(s)$ with the same coefficient formulas as in the orbitlike case.
conclusions: Z(s;P) = -1 + A \hat W_1(s) + B\hat W_2(s) + C\kappa(s)

nodes.name: The distinguished complex points $P$ for wavelike elasticae
nodes.statement: Assume $a_3\neq 0$. For $P=(\frac{b_3}{a_3},\pm \frac{i}{\sqrt{|\mu|}a_3})$ we have $$ Z(s;P) = -1 \pm i \frac{\kappa(s)}{\sqrt{|\mu|}}. $$
nodes.statement_short: For the purely imaginary choice $P=(b_3/a_3,\pm i/(\sqrt{|\mu|}a_3))$ one gets $Z=-1\pm i\kappa/\sqrt{|\mu|}$.

nodes.name: Wavelike elasticae with $a_3\neq 0$ oscillate between two circles with centers on opposite sides
nodes.statement: Assume $a_3\neq 0$. Then we have $\gamma(\R)\subset \overline{B_{R_1}(Q_1)}\sm B_{R_2}(Q_2)$ where \begin{align*} Q_1 &= \Big(\frac{b_3}{a_3},~~~\frac{\sqrt{2+2\sqrt{1-\mu}}}{|\mu| |a_3|}\Big),\qquad R_1 = \frac{\sqrt{2-\mu+2\sqrt{1-\mu}}}{|\mu| |a_3|}, \\ Q_2 &= \Big( \frac{b_3}{a_3},-\frac{\sqrt{2+2\sqrt{1-\mu}}}{|\mu| |a_3|}\Big),\qquad R_2 = \frac{\sqrt{2-\mu+2\sqrt{1-\mu}}}{|\mu| |a_3|}. \end{align*} The curve $\gamma$ touches $\partial B_{R_1}(Q_1)$ exactly when $\kappa$ attains its maximum and it touches $\partial B_{R_2}(Q_2)$ precisely when $\kappa$ attains its minimum. Moreover, we have \begin{align} \begin{aligned} \Big\{\lim_{s\to\infty} \gamma(s), \lim_{s\to -\infty} \gamma(s)\Big\} &= \partial B_{R_1}(Q_1) \cap \partial B_{R_2}(Q_2) \\ &= \Big\{ \Big(\frac{b_3}{a_3}-\frac{1}{\sqrt{|\mu|} a_3},0\Big), \Big(\frac{b_3}{a_3}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{|\mu|} a_3},0 \Big) \Big\}. \end{aligned} \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: For $a_3\neq0$ the wavelike elastica lies between two equal-radius circles centered symmetrically about the axis, and its two ends converge to $(b_3/a_3\mp 1/(\sqrt{|\mu|}a_3),0)$.
conclusions: The curve $\gamma$ touches $\partial B_{R_1}(Q_1)$ exactly when $\kappa$ attains its maximum and it touches $\partial B_{R_2}(Q_2)$ precisely when $\kappa$ attains its minimum.

nodes.name: Wavelike elasticae with $a_3=0$ lie inside a cone
nodes.statement: Assume $a_3=0$. Then the elastica $\gamma$ from Theorem~\ref{thm:explicit_formula_wavelike} satisfies $$ \gamma(\R) \subset \mathcal{C}:= \Big\{ (x,y)\in\Hh : \frac{\big|x-\frac{b_1}{a_1}\big|}{y} \leq \frac{\sqrt{2+2\sqrt{1-\mu}}}{\sqrt{|\mu|}} \Big\}. $$ It touches the boundary of the cone $\mathcal{C}$ at points where $\kappa$ attains its maximum or minimum. Moreover, we have $$ \big\{\lim_{s\to\infty} \gamma_2(s), \lim_{s\to -\infty} \gamma_2(s)\big\} = \{0,\infty\}. $$
nodes.statement_short: For $a_3=0$ the elastica stays inside the cone $\mathcal{C}$ with apex $(b_1/a_1,0)$, touching its boundary at the extrema of $\kappa$, and $\gamma_2$ tends to $0$ and $\infty$ at the two ends.
conclusions: It touches the boundary of the cone $\mathcal{C}$ at points where $\kappa$ attains its maximum or minimum.

nodes.name: Classification of the curvature functions of elasticae in $\Hh$
nodes.statement: From Table (2.7)(c) in~\cite{LanSing_the_total} for $G=-1$ we find that $\kappa$ is, up to multiplication by $-1$, one of the following functions: \begin{align*} &(i)\;\;\quad \kappa\equiv \sqrt{2} &&\mu = 1\\ &(ii)\;\quad \kappa(s) = \frac{2}{\sqrt{2-k^2}}\dn\Big(\frac{s+a}{\sqrt{2-k^2}},k\Big)\quad(0<k<1) && \mu =\frac{4(1-k^2)}{(2-k^2)^2}, \\ &(iii)\quad \kappa\equiv 0 \quad\text{or}\quad \kappa(s)= 2\sech(s+a) &&\mu= 0, \\ &(iv)\;\quad \kappa(s)= \frac{2k}{\sqrt{2k^2-1}} \cn\Big(\frac{s+a}{\sqrt{2k^2-1}},k\Big)\quad (\frac{1}{\sqrt 2}<k<1) && \mu = - \frac{4k^2(1-k^2)}{(2k^2-1)^2}. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Up to sign, $\kappa$ is one of four families: constant $\sqrt2$, a $\dn$-function, $0$ or $2\sech$, or a $\cn$-function, with $\mu$ positive, zero or negative respectively.

nodes.name: Parity, periodicity and inverses of $\sn,\cn,\dn$
nodes.statement: The function $\cn$ is even and $2K(k)-$antiperiodic, $\sn$ is odd and $2K(k)-$antiperiodic while $\dn$ is $2K(k)-$periodic. Moreover, $\sn:[-K(k),K(k)]\to [-1,1],\cn:[0,K(k)]\to [0,1]$ and $\dn:[0,K(k)]\to [\sqrt{1-k^2},1]$ are bijective with inverses given by \begin{align} \sn^{-1}(z,k) = F(z,k),\quad \cn^{-1}(z,k) = F(\sqrt{1-z^2},k),\quad \dn^{-1}(z,k) = F(\sqrt{1-z^2}/k,k). \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: $\cn,\sn$ are $2K$-antiperiodic (even/odd) and $\dn$ is $2K$-periodic; each is bijective on the natural interval with inverse expressed by $F$.

Moreover, $\sn:[-K(k),K(k)]\to [-1,1],\cn:[0,K(k)]\to [0,1]$ and $\dn:[0,K(k)]\to [\sqrt{1-k^2},1]$ are bijective with inverses given by

nodes.name: Quarter-period shift formulas for $\sn,\cn,\dn$
nodes.statement: In particular we have $\sn(K(k))=1,\cn(K(k))=0,\dn(K(k))=\sqrt{1-k^2}$ and addition formulas similar to the ones for sine and cosine can be proved. We will only need \begin{align} \cn(s-K(k)) = \sqrt{1-k^2} \frac{\sn(s)}{\dn(s)},\; \sn(s-K(k)) = -\frac{\cn(s)}{\dn(s)},\; \dn(s-K(k)) = \frac{\sqrt{1-k^2}}{\dn(s)}, \end{align} see 122.03 in \cite{ByrFri_handbook}.
nodes.statement_short: Shifting the argument by $-K(k)$ interchanges $\cn,\sn,\dn$ according to three explicit quotient formulas.

nodes.name: Partial derivatives of Heuman's Lambda function
nodes.statement: The formulas 710.11 and 730.04 imply \begin{align} \begin{aligned} \frac{\partial}{\partial l} \Lambda_0(\arcsin(l),k) &= \frac{2(E(k)-(1-k^2)l^2K(k))}{\pi l'\sqrt{1-(1-k^2)l^2}},\\ \frac{\partial}{\partial k} \Lambda_0(\arcsin(l),k) &= \frac{2(E(k)-K(k))ll'}{\pi k\sqrt{1-(1-k^2)l^2}}. \end{aligned} \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Explicit formulas for $\partial_l\Lambda_0(\arcsin l,k)$ and $\partial_k\Lambda_0(\arcsin l,k)$ in terms of $E(k),K(k)$.

nodes.name: M\"obius invariance of the curve-reconstruction ODE system
nodes.statement: This ODE system is invariant under M\"obius transformations and in particular under the continuous isometries of the hyperbolic plane where only the initial data $\gamma_1(0),\gamma_2(0),\phi(0)$ changes. Identifying $\Hh$ with $\{x+iy:y>0\}$ and writing $\gamma=\gamma_1+i\gamma_2$ these isometries take the following form: \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] horizontal translation: $\gamma\mapsto \gamma+a$ for $a\in\R$, \item[(ii)] dilation: $\gamma \mapsto b\gamma$ for $b>0$, \item[(iii)] hyperbolic rotation: $\gamma\mapsto \tfrac{\cos(\theta/2)\gamma+\sin(\theta/2)}{-\sin(\theta/2)\gamma+\cos(\theta/2)} $ for $\theta\in\R$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: The ODE system is invariant under the continuous isometries of $\Hh$: horizontal translation, dilation and hyperbolic rotation, which only change the initial data.
conclusions: This ODE system is invariant under M\"obius transformations and in particular under the continuous isometries of the hyperbolic plane where only the initial data $\gamma_1(0),\gamma_2(0),\phi(0)$ changes.

nodes.name: Ball characterization of the sublevel and superlevel sets of $Z$
nodes.statement: From the definition of $Z$ in \eqref{eq:def_Z} we deduce the following: The inequality $Z(s;P)\geq -1+\rho>0$ holds if and only if $\gamma$ lies outside the Euclidean ball with center $(P_1,\rho P_2)$ and radius $\sqrt{\rho^2-1}|P_2|$. The same way, we have $Z(s;P)\leq -1+\rho$ if and only if $\gamma$ lies inside this ball.
nodes.statement_short: $Z(s;P)\ge -1+\rho$ (resp. $\le$) holds exactly when $\gamma$ lies outside (resp. inside) the Euclidean ball with center $(P_1,\rho P_2)$ and radius $\sqrt{\rho^2-1}|P_2|$.
conclusions: The inequality $Z(s;P)\geq -1+\rho>0$ holds if and only if $\gamma$ lies outside the Euclidean ball with center $(P_1,\rho P_2)$ and radius $\sqrt{\rho^2-1}|P_2|$.
The same way, we have $Z(s;P)\leq -1+\rho$ if and only if $\gamma$ lies inside this ball.

nodes.name: Geodesics of the hyperbolic plane
nodes.statement: Geodesics in $\Hh$ are known to be either vertical lines or half circles in dependence of the initial position and angle.
nodes.section: 3 Classification of elasticae in the hyperbolic plane
conclusions: Geodesics in $\Hh$ are known to be either vertical lines or half circles in dependence of the initial position and angle.

nodes.name: Symmetry of oriented orbitlike solutions (proof of the symmetry theorem)
nodes.statement: Assume $A_1=-B_1\neq 0, A_2=B_2>0,\phi_A+\phi_B\in 2\pi\Z$ such that $$ \pm\big(\frac{A_2}{A_1}\sin(\phi_A) + \cos(\phi_A)\big) \notin (0,2). $$ Then all positively $(\pm=+)$ respectively negatively $(\pm=-)$ oriented orbitlike solutions of~\eqref{eq:DirichletBVP} are symmetric.
nodes.statement_short: Restatement and proof of the symmetry theorem: symmetric data with $\pm(\tfrac{A_2}{A_1}\sin\phi_A+\cos\phi_A)\notin(0,2)$ force every oriented orbitlike solution to be symmetric.
conclusions: Then all positively $(\pm=+)$ respectively negatively $(\pm=-)$ oriented orbitlike solutions of~\eqref{eq:DirichletBVP} are symmetric.

nodes.name: Complete solution set for $A_1=B_1=0$ and symmetry breaking
nodes.statement: Let $A_1=B_1=0,A_2=B_2>0,\phi_A=\phi_B=0$. Then all orbitlike solutions of the Dirichlet problem \eqref{eq:DirichletBVP2} are given by $$ k=k_{m,n},\; L=\mathcal{L}_{m,n},\; s_*\in\R \qquad\text{where }m,n\in\N \text{ satisfy }1<\frac{2m}{n}<\sqrt 2. $$ These solutions are symmetric if and only if $s_*\in \sqrt{2-k^2}K(k)\Z$. In particular, there are uncountably many nonsymmetric solutions.
nodes.statement_short: For $A_1=B_1=0,\phi_A=\phi_B=0$ the orbitlike solutions are exactly $k=k_{m,n},L=\mathcal{L}_{m,n},s_*\in\R$, and they are symmetric only for the countably many $s_*\in\sqrt{2-k^2}K(k)\Z$.
conclusions: Then all orbitlike solutions of the Dirichlet problem \eqref{eq:DirichletBVP2} are given by
These solutions are symmetric if and only if $s_*\in \sqrt{2-k^2}K(k)\Z$.
In particular, there are uncountably many nonsymmetric solutions.

nodes.name: Hyperbolic circles are Euclidean balls with shifted center
nodes.statement: Notice moreover that the above reasoning shows that hyperbolic circles with center $P$ and radius $\Arcosh(\rho)$ are nothing but Euclidean balls with center $(P_1,\rho P_2)$ and radius $\sqrt{\rho^2-1}|P_2|$ since both are characterized by the identity $Z(s;P)\equiv -1+\rho$, see~\eqref{eq:metric}.
nodes.statement_short: A hyperbolic circle of center $P$ and radius $\Arcosh(\rho)$ coincides with the Euclidean ball of center $(P_1,\rho P_2)$ and radius $\sqrt{\rho^2-1}|P_2|$.
conclusions: hyperbolic circles with center $P$ and radius $\Arcosh(\rho)$ are nothing but Euclidean balls with center $(P_1,\rho P_2)$ and radius $\sqrt{\rho^2-1}|P_2|$

nodes.name: Reduction of negatively oriented elasticae to positively oriented ones
nodes.statement: Notice that the analysis of an elastica $\gamma=(\gamma_1,\gamma_2)$ with curvature $-\kappa$ may be reduced to the analysis of an elastica $\gamma=M\circ (-\gamma_1,\gamma_2)$ having curvature $\kappa$ where $M$ is any of the M\"obius transformations (i),(ii),(iii) from the last section.
nodes.statement_short: Curvature $-\kappa$ reduces to curvature $\kappa$ after reflecting and applying a M\"obius transformation.
nodes.section: 3 Classification of elasticae in the hyperbolic plane
conclusions: the analysis of an elastica $\gamma=(\gamma_1,\gamma_2)$ with curvature $-\kappa$ may be reduced to the analysis of an elastica $\gamma=M\circ (-\gamma_1,\gamma_2)$ having curvature $\kappa$

nodes.name: Selfintersections of $\gamma_{m,n}$ are simple
nodes.statement: Our computations even reveal that these intersections are simple in the sense that for any given such $s$ there is precisely one $t\in (s,\mathcal{L}_{m,n})$ with $\gamma(s)=\gamma(t)$. We remark that in the nonclosed case essentially the same proof shows that the elasticae selfintersect infinitely many times.
nodes.statement_short: Each selfintersection parameter $s$ has exactly one partner $t$, and nonclosed orbitlike elasticae selfintersect infinitely often.
conclusions: these intersections are simple in the sense that for any given such $s$ there is precisely one $t\in (s,\mathcal{L}_{m,n})$ with $\gamma(s)=\gamma(t)$
in the nonclosed case essentially the same proof shows that the elasticae selfintersect infinitely many times

nodes.name: The catenoid is an accumulation set in the limit $2m_n/n\to 1$
nodes.statement: Similarly, one can study the limit $2m_n/n\to 1$, which corresponds to $k_{m_n}\to 1$. In this case Proposition~\ref{prop:enclosures} tells us that there is no Hausdorff convergence at all, but the catenoid is, as a subset of $\Hh$, contained in the set of accumlation points of the curves $\gamma_{m_n,n}(\R)$. The latter follows from the fact that the solution of the initial value problem~\eqref{eq:ODE_solution} converges locally (but not globally) uniformly towards the catenoid solution as the curvature functions approach $\sqrt 2 \sech(s)$ locally uniformly.
nodes.statement_short: As $2m_n/n\to1$ there is no Hausdorff convergence, but the catenoid lies in the accumulation set of the curves $\gamma_{m_n,n}(\R)$.
conclusions: there is no Hausdorff convergence at all, but the catenoid is, as a subset of $\Hh$, contained in the set of accumlation points of the curves $\gamma_{m_n,n}(\R)$

nodes.name: Willmore Conjecture
nodes.statement: Notably the Willmore Conjecture says that the infimum of the Willmore energy in the class of immersed tori in $\R^3$ is achieved by the Clifford-Torus. It has been an open problem for about fifty years and its proof due to Marques and Neves \cite{MarNev_Wilconj} must be considered as a breakthrough in the study of Willmore surfaces.
nodes.statement_short: The Clifford torus minimizes the Willmore energy among immersed tori in $\R^3$; proved by Marques and Neves.
nodes.section: 3 Classification of elasticae in the hyperbolic plane
conclusions: the infimum of the Willmore energy in the class of immersed tori in $\R^3$ is achieved by the Clifford-Torus

nodes.name: All closed orbitlike elasticae are unstable
nodes.statement: and the natural conjecture is that all closed orbitlike elasticae are unstable.
conclusions: all closed orbitlike elasticae are unstable

nodes.name: Existence of nonsymmetric or nongraphical solutions of the Willmore Dirichlet problem
nodes.statement: Using this approach several results for mostly symmetric (i.e. even) profile functions satisfying symmetric boundary value problems could be proved whereas the existence of nonsymmetric or nongraphical solutions for symmetric or nonsymmetric boundary value problems is almost completely open up to now. Our intention is to close this gap.
nodes.statement_short: Existence of nonsymmetric or nongraphical solutions for symmetric or nonsymmetric boundary data was essentially open.

nodes.name: Link between the least-energy symmetry result and the $4\pi$ energy threshold
nodes.statement: A link between these results is unfortunately missing up to now so that have to leave this issue open.

nodes.name: Dirichlet problem for Willmore surfaces of revolution
nodes.statement: The problem then is to find a Willmore surface with preassigned initial or end positions and angles, i.e. for given $(A_1,A_2),(B_1,B_2)$ in the hyperbolic plane and $\phi_A,\phi_B\in\R$ one has to find an elastic curve $\gamma$ with (unknown) hyperbolic length $L$ such that the following holds: \begin{equation} \mathcal{W}'(\Sigma_\gamma)=0,\quad \gamma(0)=(A_1,A_2),\quad \gamma(L)=(B_1,B_2),\quad e^{i\phi(0)}=e^{i\phi_A},\quad e^{i\phi(L)}=e^{i\phi_B}. \end{equation} Here, we formally write $\mathcal{W}'(\Sigma_\gamma)=0$ in place of the Willmore equation and the angle function $\phi$ is given by $\gamma'=|\gamma'|e^{i\phi}$.
nodes.statement_short: Find an elastica $\gamma$ of unknown hyperbolic length $L$ with $\mathcal{W}'(\Sigma_\gamma)=0$ and prescribed endpoints and angles.

nodes.name: Dirichlet problem for orbitlike elasticae
nodes.statement: Using the natural parametrization of elasticae this amounts to solving the equations \begin{equation} \mathcal{W}'(\Sigma_\gamma)=0,\quad \gamma(0)=(A_1,A_2),\quad \gamma(L)=(B_1,B_2),\quad e^{i\phi(0)}=e^{i\phi_A},\quad e^{i\phi(L)}=e^{i\phi_B} \end{equation} for given initial/end positions $(A_1,A_2),(B_1,B_2)\in \Hh$ and directions measured by $\phi_A,\phi_B\in\R$.
nodes.statement_short: The same Dirichlet system, restricted to positively oriented orbitlike elasticae, in the arclength parametrization.

nodes.name: Explicit parametrization of the Clifford torus generator
nodes.statement: One explicit parametrization of the Clifford torus is given by \begin{align*} \gamma(s) = \Big( \frac{(1+\sqrt{2})\sin(s)}{\sqrt{2}+\cos(s)}, \frac{1+\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{2}+\cos(s)}\Big),\quad e^{i\phi(s)} = \frac{1+\sqrt{2}\cos(s)+i\cdot \sin(s)}{\sqrt{2}+\cos(s)}. \end{align*} This precise realization of the Clifford torus corresponds to solving \eqref{eq:ODE_solution} for $\gamma(0)=(0,1),\phi(0)=0$ and $\kappa\equiv \sqrt{2}$.
nodes.statement_short: The circular elastica with $\kappa\equiv\sqrt2$ and $\gamma(0)=(0,1),\phi(0)=0$ generates the Clifford torus.
nodes.section: 3 Classification of elasticae in the hyperbolic plane

nodes.name: Explicit geodesics through $(0,1)$
nodes.statement: If $\phi(0)\in (\pm \frac{\pi}{2}+2\pi)\Z$ then the geodesic through $(0,1)$ is vertical and given by $\gamma(s)=(0,e^{\pm s}),\phi(s)=\phi(0)$. Otherwise, for instance in case $\phi(0)=0$, we find the halfcircles $$ \gamma(s) = (\tanh(s),\sech(s)),\qquad e^{i\phi(s)}= \sech(s) - i\cdot \tanh(s). $$
nodes.statement_short: Vertical geodesic $(0,e^{\pm s})$ and the halfcircle $(\tanh s,\sech s)$.
nodes.section: 3 Classification of elasticae in the hyperbolic plane

nodes.name: The catenoid as the asymptotically geodesic family
nodes.statement: The third exceptional family of elasticae is the asymptotically geodesic one which corresponds to the conformal class of the catenoid. By definition, it is the graph of the $\cosh$-function and therefore $$ \gamma(s) = (s,\cosh(s)),\qquad e^{i\phi(s)} = \sech(s)+i\cdot \tanh(s). $$
nodes.statement_short: The asymptotically geodesic elastica is the $\cosh$-graph $\gamma(s)=(s,\cosh(s))$, generating the catenoid.
nodes.section: 3 Classification of elasticae in the hyperbolic plane

nodes.name: Only $\gamma_{12,17}$ from the table is provably unstable
nodes.statement: Only one of the curves $\gamma_{m,n}$ listed in Table \ref{table:elasticae} (namely for $n=17,m=12$) can be proved to be unstable via Lemma~\ref{lem:instability}.

nodes.name: Nonsingular fourth-order ODE for $Z$ and the Euclidean analogue
nodes.statement: ~ \begin{itemize} \item[(a)] Differentiating \eqref{eq:ODE_Z} twice one finds $2Z^{(iv)} + \big((3\kappa^2-4)Z'\big)' + (2-\kappa^2)(Z+1) =0$. This ODE is, in contrast to \eqref{eq:ODE_Z}, not singular at zeros of $\kappa$. In particular $Z$ is smooth even in the wavelike case where $\kappa$ has infinitely many zeros. Since we will not make use of this ODE we omit the proof. \item[(b)] A similar result may be shown for elastic curves in the Euclidean plane that have recently been studied in \cite{DecGru_bvp,Man_bvp}. Such curves $\hat\gamma$, now parametrized by Euclidean arclength with curvature $\hat\kappa$, satisfy $\hat \kappa \hat Z''-2\hat\kappa'\hat Z'= const$ where $\hat Z(s):= (\gamma_1(s)-P_1)^2+(\gamma_2(s)-P_2)^2$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Differentiating the $Z$-ODE twice gives a nonsingular fourth-order ODE valid also at zeros of $\kappa$; an analogous identity holds for Euclidean elasticae.
nodes.section: 3 Classification of elasticae in the hyperbolic plane

nodes.name: Typo in the curvature function of Langer and Singer's Theorem 3
nodes.statement: Notice that $\kappa=\kappa_0 \cn^2(rs,p)$ is a typo in \cite{LanSing_Curves_in_the} since the curvature function is basically a $\dn$-function (cf. \eqref{eq:def_kappa_orbitlike}), as we will see later.

nodes.name: The winding number and selfintersection counts are missing in the literature
nodes.statement: The proof of the above theorem is in parts provided in the paper \cite{LanSing_the_total}. Computations of the winding number and of the number of selfintersections are, however, missing, so that our proofs provided later may be of interest.

nodes.name: Non-simple generating curves and nongraphical surfaces are allowed
nodes.statement: We stress that we do not impose $\gamma$ to be simple so that the generated surface $\Sigma_\gamma$ may not be embedded. In particular, in contrast to most of the earlier works on the Dirichlet problem for Willmore surfaces of revolution, we do not assume that $\Sigma_\gamma$ has a global parametrization as a graph (which in fact only occurs in very special situations).

nodes.name: Properties of the symmetry-breaking solutions
nodes.statement: The proof of Theorem~\ref{thm:Symmetry_breaking} reveals further properties of the constructed solutions. We will see that one can choose $A_1=B_1=0$, $A_2=B_2>0$ and $\phi_A=-\phi_B=0$ and that the conformal class of every $\gamma_{m,n}$ $(m,n\in\N)$ described in Theorem~\ref{thm:LanSin} contains uncountably many nonsymmetric representatives that solve the Dirichlet problem~\eqref{eq:DirichletBVP}. Examples are illustrated in Figure~\ref{Fig:Symmetry_breaking}.
nodes.statement_short: The nonsymmetric solutions can be realized with $A_1=B_1=0$, and every conformal class $\gamma_{m,n}$ contains uncountably many of them.

nodes.name: Sign convention for the hyperbolic curvature
nodes.statement: Here, we chose this sign convention for $\kappa$ in order to be consistent with (2.3) in \cite{DalAcDecGru_Classical_solutions}.

nodes.name: The remaining isometries are discrete reflections
nodes.statement: The missing isometries are discrete and come from reflections, i.e. horizontal reflection and inversion with respect to the unit sphere. Notice that both cause a sign change in the curvature function.

nodes.name: Jacobi's elliptic functions in the study of elastic knots
nodes.statement: We mention that Jacobi's elliptic functions also appear in the study of elastic knots \cite{LanSing_Knotted}, \cite{IvSin_knot_types}. In the following we concentrate on elasticae generated by curvature functions given by the above formulas.
nodes.section: 3 Classification of elasticae in the hyperbolic plane

nodes.name: Reduced versions of the Willmore conjecture
nodes.statement: Reduced versions of this conjecture were proved in \cite{LanSing_Curves_in_the} (Corollary~5) within the class of Willmore surfaces of revolution and in the larger class of canal surfaces of torus type in \cite{HerJerPin_Beweis}.
nodes.section: 3 Classification of elasticae in the hyperbolic plane

nodes.name: Theta function identities used later
nodes.statement: Exploiting the corresponding properties for ordinary sine and cosine (defined in the complex plane) the above functions inherit symmetry properties and further identities such as $\Theta(z+K(k),k)=\Theta_1(z,k)$ listed on page 315f. in \cite{ByrFri_handbook}. We will give a precise reference when required.

nodes.name: The two expressions for $\Delta\theta_k$ of Langer and Singer disagree
nodes.statement: We mention that Langer and Singer gave two expressions for $\Delta\theta_k$ on page 21 in \cite{LanSing_the_total} which, however, do not coincide. We chose the correct second expression as a definition. In their first expression the factor $(1-p^2)$ has to replaced by $\sqrt{1-p^2}$, as we will see in the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:properties_vartheta_orbitlike}.
nodes.statement_short: Of the two expressions for $\Delta\theta_k$ in Langer-Singer only the second is correct; the first needs $(1-p^2)$ replaced by $\sqrt{1-p^2}$.

nodes.name: $w''+2\dn^2 w=0$ is a special case of the Lam\'e equation
nodes.statement: We remark that the equation $w''+2\dn^2(\cdot,k)w=0$ is a special case ($h=2,n=1$) of the so-called Lam\'{e} equation which is typically written in the form $w''=(n(n+1)k^2\sn^2(\cdot,k)-h)w$, where $h$ is called the Lam\'{e} eigenvalue. Its significance for elastic curves and knots was pointed out by Ivey and Singer \cite{IvSin_knot_types}. We refer to \cite{Ince_the_periodic} and to Whittaker's book \cite{Whit_modern_analysis} for more information about Lam\'{e}'s equation.
nodes.statement_short: The ODE for $w_1,w_2$ is the Lam\'e equation with $h=2,n=1$; its relevance for elastic curves is due to Ivey and Singer.

nodes.name: The formula for $\vartheta'$ also appears in Bryant and Griffiths
nodes.statement: The formula for $\vartheta'$ given above can also be found on p.565 in the paper of Bryant and Griffiths \cite{BryGri_Reduction}. The derivation of this formula, however, is not carried out in detail so that our proof in section~\ref{subsec:proof_propositions_orbitlike} may be of interest.

nodes.name: An orbitlike elastica is determined by three coefficients
nodes.statement: Theorem~\ref{thm:explicit_formula_orbitlike} shows that an orbitlike elastica with curvature is determined by fixing the three coefficients $a_1,a_2,b_3$. This is not surprising given the fact that the solutions of~\eqref{eq:ODE_solution} are uniquely determined by fixing three initial conditions for $\gamma_1,\gamma_2,\phi$.

nodes.name: Eichmann determined the enclosing circles by a different method
nodes.statement: We point out that Eichmann determined the parameters of these circles with a different method without knowing explicit formulas for the elasticae, see section~5.4 in~\cite{Eich_nonuniqueness}.

nodes.name: The energies $\mathcal{W}_{m,n}$ exceed the Li-Yau lower bounds
nodes.statement: Given that all selfintersections of the $\gamma_{m,n}$ are simple, the energy levels $\mathcal{W}_{m,n}$ are much higher than the lower bounds given by the Li--Yau inequality from Theorem~6 in~\cite{LiYau_conformal}.

nodes.name: Typo in formula 361.01 of Byrd and Friedman
nodes.statement: We remark that 361.01 in \cite{ByrFri_handbook} contains a typo: $E(u)$ has to be replaced by $E(\sn(u,k),k)$ in our notation and by $E(\arcsin(\sn u),k)$ in the notation used in \cite{ByrFri_handbook}.

nodes.name: Scope and possible improvements of the instability criterion
nodes.statement: This criterion proves the instability of infinitely many of the $\gamma_{m,n}$ but also infinitely many of them are not covered. Only one of the curves $\gamma_{m,n}$ listed in Table \ref{table:elasticae} (namely for $n=17,m=12$) can be proved to be unstable via Lemma~\ref{lem:instability}. Notice that the above criterion only works for $C(k)>0$ and this is only the case for $0\leq k<0.6869145$. With more computational effort the instability of more curves $\gamma_{m,n}$ can be shown both analytically and numerically. For instance it is possible to analytically determine the constrained minimizer of $I$ in the set of functions $\phi$ given by $$ \phi(s)=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1} a_j \cos\Big( \frac{js}{T}\Big) + \sum_{j=1}^{n-1} b_j \sin\Big( \frac{js}{T}\Big). $$ A reasonable constraint is given by $a_0^2+b_0^2+\ldots+a_{n-1}^2+b_{n-1}^2=1$. The constrained minimizers are of the form $a_j \cos\big(\frac{js}{T}\big)+a_{n-j}\cos\big(\frac{(n-j)s}{T }\big)$ or $b_j \sin\big(\frac{js}{T}\big)+b_{n-j}\sin\big(\frac{(n-j)s}{T }\big)$ for some $j\in\{1,\ldots,n-1\}$ so that there is a higher chance to find negative values for $I_{m,n}(\phi)$. However, the analytical expressions for these minima are much more complicated than the one from Lemma \ref{lem:instability} and we could not detect any substantial gain with respect to the monochromatic ansatz functions when applying the resulting criterion to elasticae with large $k$. Numerically, one clearly obtains much better results by choosing sufficiently large test function spaces
nodes.statement_short: The monochromatic criterion only works for $C(k)>0$, i.e. $k<0.6869145$; richer test-function spaces improve it numerically but not substantially analytically.

nodes.name: Shape of the surfaces approximating the Clifford torus
nodes.statement: The consequence is that the Clifford torus may be well approximated by orbitlike surfaces of revolutions the shape of which, however, becomes more and more complicated as they approach the torus.

nodes.name: The proof of the wavelike $W_1,W_2$ identities is omitted
nodes.statement: As in the orbitlike case we collect some properties of $W_1,W_2,\kappa$. Since the proof is completely analogous to the one of Proposition~\ref{prop:W1W2_orbitlike} and the validity of the identities may be checked using a computer, we omit it.

nodes.name: The wavelike formula for $\vartheta'$ also appears in Bryant and Griffiths
nodes.statement: We mention that the formula for $\vartheta'$ also appears on p.569 in \cite{BryGri_Reduction}, but no detailed proof is given there.

nodes.name: Oscillation of wavelike elasticae around a halfcircle or a cone axis
nodes.statement: So we conclude as in \cite{LanSing_the_total} that wavelike elasticae with $a_3\neq 0$ oscillate around the halfcircle around $(b_3/a_3,0)$ with radius $1/(\sqrt{|\mu|}a_3)$. As we show now, a somewhat similar phenomenon occurs in the case $a_3=0$ . Here, $\gamma$ is an unbounded curve lying inside a cone with apex $(b_1/a_1,0)$ and opening angle $2\arctan( \sqrt{2+2\sqrt{1-\mu}}/\sqrt{|\mu|})$ and it oscillates around the vertical axis of the cone, see Figure~\ref{Fig:orbitlike_oscillations} or Fig.~3 in the Eichmann's paper \cite{Eich_nonuniqueness} where the same phenomenon has been observed. The precise statement for the case $a_3=0$ is the following:
nodes.statement_short: Wavelike elasticae with $a_3\neq0$ oscillate about a halfcircle; for $a_3=0$ they oscillate about the axis of a cone with apex $(b_1/a_1,0)$.

nodes.name: The $l$-dependence of the second Dirichlet equation can be made explicit
nodes.statement: We remark that the dependency of the equation \eqref{Gl:DirProblem_II} with respect to $l$ can be made ''more explicit'' because of $\vartheta(s+2l\sqrt{2-k^2}K(k))=\vartheta(s)+l\Delta\theta_k$ for all $s\in\R$, see Proposition~\ref{prop:properties_vartheta_orbitlike}~(ii).

nodes.name: Proof of the ODE for the conformal invariant $Z$
nodes.statement: For convenience we write $Z:=Z(\cdot;P)$. Differentiating $Z$ gives the formula \begin{equation} Z' = \frac{\gamma_1-P_1}{P_2} \cdot \cos(\phi) + \frac{\gamma_2^2-P_2^2-(\gamma_1-P_1)^2}{2P_2\gamma_2}\cdot \sin(\phi). \end{equation} Differentiating once more and using $\phi'+\cos(\phi)=\kappa$ gives \begin{align*} Z'' &= \phi'\cdot \Big( - \frac{\gamma_1-P_1}{P_2}\cdot \sin(\phi) + \frac{\gamma_2^2-P_2^2-(\gamma_1-P_1)^2}{2P_2\gamma_2}\cdot\cos(\phi) \Big) \\ &\quad + \frac{\gamma_1'}{P_2}\cos(\phi) + \frac{2\gamma_2^2\gamma_2'-2(\gamma_1-P_1)\gamma_2\gamma_1' - (\gamma_2^2-P_2^2-(\gamma_1-P_1)^2)\gamma_2' }{2P_2\gamma_2^2} \sin(\phi) \\ &= (\kappa-\cos(\phi)) \cdot \Big( - \frac{\gamma_1-P_1}{P_2}\cdot \sin(\phi) + \frac{\gamma_2^2-P_2^2-(\gamma_1-P_1)^2}{2P_2\gamma_2}\cdot\cos(\phi) \Big) \\ &\quad + \frac{\gamma_2}{P_2}\cdot \cos^2(\phi) + \frac{(\gamma_2^2+P_2^2+ (\gamma_1-P_1)^2) \sin(\phi) -2(\gamma_1-P_1)\gamma_2\cos(\phi)}{2P_2\gamma_2} \cdot \sin(\phi) \\ &= (\kappa-\cos(\phi)) \cdot \Big( - \frac{\gamma_1-P_1}{P_2}\cdot \sin(\phi) + \frac{\gamma_2^2-P_2^2-(\gamma_1-P_1)^2}{2P_2\gamma_2}\cdot\cos(\phi) \Big) \\ &\quad + \frac{\gamma_2}{P_2}\cdot \cos^2(\phi) + \frac{\gamma_2^2+P_2^2+(\gamma_1-P_1)^2}{2P_2\gamma_2} \cdot \sin^2(\phi) -\frac{\gamma_1-P_1}{P_2}\cdot \sin(\phi)\cos(\phi) \\ &= \frac{\gamma_2^2+P_2^2+(\gamma_1-P_1)^2}{2P_2\gamma_2} - \kappa w \\ &= Z+1-\kappa w. \end{align*} Here, the auxiliary function $w$ is given by $$ w : = \frac{\gamma_1-P_1}{P_2} \cdot \sin(\phi) - \frac{\gamma_2^2-P_2^2-(\gamma_1-P_1)^2}{2P_2\gamma_2} \cdot \cos(\phi). $$ From the identity \begin{align*} w' &= \Big(\frac{\gamma_1-P_1}{P_2} \cdot \cos(\phi) + \frac{\gamma_2^2-P_2^2-(\gamma_1-P_1)^2}{2P_2\gamma_2}\cdot \sin(\phi) \Big) \phi' \\ &\;+ \Big( \frac{\gamma_2}{P_2}\cdot \sin(\phi) - \Big(\frac{\gamma_2^2-P_2^2-(\gamma_1-P_1)^2}{2P_2\gamma_2}\Big)'\Big) \cdot \cos(\phi) \\ &= \Big(\frac{\gamma_1-P_1}{P_2} \cdot \cos(\phi) + \frac{\gamma_2^2-P_2^2-(\gamma_1-P_1)^2}{2P_2\gamma_2}\cdot \sin(\phi) \Big) \phi' \\ &\;+ \Big(\frac{\gamma_1-P_1}{P_2} \cdot \cos(\phi) + \frac{\gamma_2^2-P_2^2-(\gamma_1-P_1)^2}{2P_2\gamma_2}\cdot \sin(\phi) \Big) \cos(\phi) \\ &= Z' (\phi'+\cos(\phi)) \\ &= \kappa Z' \end{align*} we get \begin{align*} (\kappa Z''-2\kappa'Z'+\kappa Z + \kappa)' &= (-\kappa^2 w-2\kappa'Z'+ 2\kappa Z + 2\kappa)' \\ &= Z'(-2\kappa''+2\kappa) -2\kappa^2w' + 2\kappa' (- \kappa w -Z'' + Z+1) \\ &\stackrel{\eqref{eq:ODE_kappa}}{=} Z'(-2\kappa''+2\kappa-\kappa^3) \\ &= 0 \end{align*} so that $\kappa Z''-2\kappa'Z'+\kappa Z + \kappa$ must be constant.
